speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREE- MENTS WITH INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that yesterday representatives of the governments of India and Canada concluded and initialed in Ottawa two agreements in the atomic energy field of far reaching significance to both countries. An announcement along this line is being made in New Delhi today. These agreements will be formally signed in New Delhi shortly, and I shall table them at that time.
One of these agreements provides for extensive technical co-operation between the atomic energy authorities of the two countries. Valuable information already developed as a result of Canada's special experience in heavy water power reactor systems will be transferred to the government of India for full commercial use in India. This information, which has been valued by the government of India at $5 million, is to be supplied without cost to India and without deduction from Colombo plan or other assistance.
Under the other agreement between the two governments Canada and India will co-operate in the construction of a nuclear power station of the Candu type with a net electrical output of 200 megawatts to be located in Rajasthan state in India. The government of Canada will provide credit facilities for the purchase of services, material and equipment supplied from Canada, which are estimated to cost approximately $35 million out of a total cost of about $70 million.
Half of the initial charge of uranium fuel for this reactor will be procured from Canada. At current prices this half supply would be worth approximately $2.1 million. Canada will also supply such additional fuel for the station as may be required by India from time to time, provided that Canadian fuel is not more expensive than any other foreign fuel.
Canada and India have agreed to exchange information regarding the operation of this station and its counterpart, the Douglas Point nuclear generating station now under construction in Canada. They have also agreed that the two stations shall be used only for peaceful purposes, and the agreement includes appropriate provisions to this end.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The two agreements reflect the longstanding co-operation between Canada and India in the peaceful uses of atomic energy and will further strengthen the close and friendly relations between the two countries.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on the amendment.
At first glance, I would say the motion is out of order since it substitutes a new proposal to the one under consideration. At any rate, if we were to recognize the principle stated in the proposal, the province of Quebec would lose the advantages it could derive from the motion moved by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen). In fact, it is because the former Quebec government refused to participate in this program, that technical and vocational training is behind the times in that province.
The purpose of this government proposal is to give equal treatment to Quebec and other provinces which did not, due to special circumstances, fully benefit from this legislation.
In my opinion the proposal made by the hon. member for Quebec East would destroy that equality, and I am sure that consequence escaped his mind, but the fact remains that such would be the result.
The hon. member's motion is a mere statement which does not affect the measure now before us, but should the principles to be drawn from it be inserted in the proposed legislation, the benefit of equality being sought for the province of Quebec would be removed.
For that reason, and also in order to avoid the inconvenience of having to ask the chairman to give a decision which, in my opinion, would have to be against the motion, I hope the hon. member who made that proposal which, personally, I find quite acceptable in its general terms, but which nevertheless remains an amendment to the motion now under discussion, will agree to withdraw his own motion.

I had the opportunity to study the proposal made yesterday by the hon. member for Quebec East. I naturally listened closely to the comments made by the hon. members of this committee during the discussion which just took place.
In the first place, I think that the proposed amendment is out of order in its present form. It seems to me that the object of an amendment is to alter the main motion and that it can be introduced, according to citation No. 201 of Beauchesne's fourth edition by one of the three following procedures:
(a)	by leaving out certain words;
(b)	by leaving out certain words in order to insert other words;
(c)	by inserting or adding other words.
Besides, I think that an amendment must be related to the motion it tends to modify, that is to say that the substance of that amendment must not only refer to the substance of the main motion, but also be directed towards the main motion and fall within its provisions and details.
Generally speaking, an amendment should tend to restrict rather than to enlarge upon the terms of the main motion.
I feel therefore that not only is the motion out of order in its present form, but that it is defective in that it does not fall within the framework I just mentioned. Consequently,
Vocational Training Assistance Act it is not germane to the resolution put by the minister.
That being the case, I think the hon. member's proposal is really a substantive motion and that, as such, it cannot be acted on before the notice prescribed in that respect has been given, and that when the Speaker is in the chair.
If my conclusions are right, I think that the hon. member's proposal departs from the terms of standing order 44, namely:
44. When a question is under debate no motion is received unless to amend it; to postpone it to a day certain; for the previous question; for reading the orders of the day; for proceeding to another order; to adjourn the debate; or for the adjournment of the house.
I do not suggest that all these procedures would be acceptable when the house sits in committee of the whole. I suggest that the motion of the hon. member is inconsistent with any or all of the provisions of standing order 44.
Consequently, for the reasons indicated and having considered the arguments put forward this morning, I regret to tell the hon. member for Quebec East that his motion is not in order at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to discuss this resolution I think I should first point out that I know I am the second speaker on the Conservative side, and so I

disagree with the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway who said there was going to be just one speaker from each party. I have some views which I want to communicate with regard to this resolution, and I thought it better to do so on the resolution stage than on any other.
Second, I confess I am quite at a loss to understand the objections of the hon. member for Quebec East. He seems to feel that the original act, and the modifications which the resolution suggests, are unjust toward Quebec in that they were made for the English speaking provinces. I must say I am unable to see this argument at all. It is true Quebec has used only a very small portion of the money available to it, but Quebec is not the only province in that situation. My own province, Saskatchewan, has used a surprisingly small portion of the money that was available, and so I cannot see his objections.
The resolution contains four provisions. The first two, increasing the federal percentage of training allowances for unemployed persons, and for training allowances for employed persons in industry, should make it possible for the provinces to increase the aid they are now giving in these two fields. The third provision, which extends the date for payment of the 75 per cent of capital costs, should enable the provinces that were less ready to take advantage of federal assistance to do so now, provinces like Quebec and Saskatchewan.
Of course I support, as I think do all hon. members, these three provisions. It is very easy for a Conservative to support them, since they merely continue and extend to some degree legislation which the previous government introduced in December, 1960; legislation which I feel certain would have been imaginatively and constructively improved by this time rather than merely continued.
The original bill demonstrated the Conservative party's belief that skilled manpower is of prime importance in fostering national development. This principle is recognized in other countries, and in fact the Labour party in Britain intends to fight the next election on this premise. They believe that the future of Britain depends upon establishing a well educated class of workmen, with a large and well trained group of scientists creating the new products and the new processes which will provide the jobs for these super workmen. Surely we believe in the same thing.
As the hon. member for Cape Breton South said in the House of Commons on December 9, 1960, speaking to the original bill:
Anyone who has studied the bill will have to admit it is the most positive step forward in the training field ever taken in this country.

It was the previous government which had the imagination to take this step, and coupled with that imagination concern for the people and the welfare of the country to produce this fine piece of legislation. I believe I should also add that it had the administrative skill to make the bill work effectively, administrative skill which the present session has demonstrated is so sadly lacking in this government.
The legislation which was then introduced empowered the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces to provide financial assistance toward the costs of providing technical and vocational training programs for adults. This was quite a change and enlargement in assistance. Formerly programs of technical and vocational training were available only to unemployed persons, students in technical and vocational courses in secondary schools, apprentices, supervisors in industry, and disabled persons.
Therefore we see that in December, 1960, for the first time the Progressive Conservative government produced legislation which enabled it to share in the costs of providing the necessary technical and vocational training to persons who required skills to work as technicians, to persons over regular school leaving age who needed training to develop or increase occupational skills and, third, to teachers, supervisors or administrators who were to carry out the training programs.
While providing this assistance to the provinces to train these people, the previous government also recognized the need to provide funds so that additional training facilities could be provided across Canada. Thus the government provided contributions of up to 75 per cent of the capital cost of such facilities and equipment. These new facilities included technical and vocational schools, technical institutes and trade schools.
The need for such legislation was very great. It was a need that had existed for a long time during the governing years of the previous Liberal administration, and the program meeting this need was tremendously successful. More than 450 projects, involving 221 completely new vocational high schools, trade schools or technical institutes were constructed. In all accommodation was provided for some 130,000 more technical and vocational students. The estimated cost of these approved projects was in the neighbourhood of $442 million, and that $442 million was one of the reasons that the Conservative administration had such large deficits during its period in office. I for one, and I am sure many other Canadians, applaud deficits like these, deficits which educate our people, deficits which help to assure a fine future for our country.
Vocational Training Assistance Act
Besides doing this, the previous government paid 75 per cent of the cost of training unemployed persons. It also shared with the provinces, on a 50-50 basis, the operational cost, including student allowances, of approved training programs. That Progressive Conservative government provided 50 per cent of the cost of training programs for apprentices, disabled persons and supervisors in industry. This was done because the previous government believed that industry itself must accept a larger share of the responsibility for the establishment of suitable training programs to meet its own needs. Provision was made to assist industry in this regard to develop active training programs in (1) apprenticeship training, (2) the utilization of training facilities in industrial establishments for training unemployed persons, (3) the enlargement of present programs for training instructors in industry, and (4) the introduction of new training programs by industry to upgrade the skills of employees to meet continuing manpower needs and changing occupational requirements.
All that the resolution now before the house will do is increase to some extent the financial contributions and, more significantly, extend the April 1, 1963 time limit on federal contributions to capital costs of training facilities built by the provinces to March 31, 1967. The resolution also introduces a limiting factor in that no province can receive more than $480 per student in the 15 to 19 years of age training group. The apparent reason behind this move is that the old time limit discriminated in favour of the provinces where technical and vocational training was well advanced.
The $480 limitation is one feature of the resolution which disturbs me. There is quite evidently no attempt to apply the equalization of educational opportunity principle to the financial provisions. In brief this principle is that every Canadian should have an equal right to a good education. It is equally obvious that all provinces are not equally capable financially of providing this right. It should therefore be the purpose of the federal government to provide financial support for those least able to provide it themselves. In other words, Mr. Chairman, I believe very strongly that it should be an axiom of federal aid in all educational fields to provide funds which will enable every Canadian to have that equal educational opportunity. I am afraid that by bringing every province's aid up to the limit set, the need of those who require it most is not being recognized.
I would like to quote from a report in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of recent date on comments made by Dr. J. T. Montague, director of the industrial relations institute at the

Vocational Training Assistance Act University of British Columbia, which I believe emphasizes the main fault of a program such as this resolution presents. This article is headed "Roundhouse blows at ill defined target" and says:
"The federal government has dashed to the scene with answers which show strong conviction about the trends which are evolving"-
Then further:
But, Dr. Montague said, "Indications of change in the labour force are seemingly without sufficient pattern from which to picture clearly the labour force of the future.
"Firm answers have taken hold in an area where it is next to impossible to describe anything more than the most general labour force adjustments needed to meet industrial adjustments which as yet are without definite shape".
The article continues:
"Even a quick glimpse leaves me spinning in questions of whether we will find in the long run that today's efforts have assisted in overcoming structural difficulties within the labour force or whether, by carrying out single-skill programs which are often dead-end in character, we have guaranteed to complicate the future".
Programs set up under this act are not designed to correct the root of the matter. Only the establishment of an efficient, widely based, general educational program designed to raise the educational level of our people to the highest in the world is good enough for this country. Some of the provinces may be able to do this for themselves, but unless all the provinces do it this country will continually be plagued by an overabundance of cheap, uneducated, unskilled labour; and all labour, all people, all provinces, rich and poor, will suffer from a depreciated standard of living as a consequence.
In this respect, Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer to what the hon. lady from Northumberland said on Friday, October 25. I will not actually quote her words but will merely paraphrase them. She spoke of the fact that over 1,700,000 of the residents of the 17 metropolitan areas came from other countries, and almost one million of the residents of those 17 cities came from a province other than that in which their respective city was located. The implication should be obvious to the wealthy metropolitan areas. They should, in their own interests, have no objection to assisting in the education of the less fortunate. This is recognized by the school trustees association, which recently presented a brief to the royal commission on taxation which contained a number of practical suggestions. I again quote from a report in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of recent date:
The federal government must make more tax dollars available to lower levels of government if the ballooning costs of education are to be met, the Canadian school trustees association said today.
[Mr. Cantelon.l

The article says further:
The association recommended that local government be given the responsibility for elementary education, with necessary assistance from provincial governments which would also take care of secondary education. Higher and vocational education would be looked after by the federal government. Additional assistance should be given to the Atlantic provinces, and any other provinces that need it, to help bring expenditures per pupil in line with the national average.
These are good, concrete suggestions, and no matter what may be the expressed opinions of some members about the interference of the federal parliament in the rights of the provinces, I contend that help given to universities and help given to the provinces for improvements in vocational and technical education does not interfere with provincial rights. We are doing it now, and no one can honestly say that the dominion has in any way interfered in provincial control of education by offering financial aid where it was badly needed.
I would like to conclude by saying that I am quite disappointed that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has not yet presented his bill for the granting of 10,000 scholarships. Surely he is not worried about the cost, because this government seems willing to spend money on almost anything else; the deficit grows by leaps and bounds. Surely this program is not being delayed because the government is suddenly growing parsimonious. There are so many other places in which millions of dollars could be cut off, with less loss to the country. For example, the new Department of Industry is to have some 125 executive employees each drawing over $11,000 a year, for a total of $1,500,000 yearly. The enlargement of a high priced bureaucracy is proceeded with apace, but the education of our people is relegated to a minor position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: CURRENCY, MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AUTHORIZATION TO PURCHASE SECURITIES OF INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I wish to thank members of all parties opposite for their very generous agreement to allow me to make a purely explanatory statement concerning this motion and move on to second reading of the bill with the minimum of debate. My statement will be slightly longer than would ordinarily be the case at this stage in order that the purpose of the legislation may be made quite clear, to the end that this explanation may assist hon. members opposite by indicating what the government intends to achieve by the proposed legislation.
Under the provisions of section 22 of the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act the exchange fund is permitted to acquire and to hold certain types of foreign assets. At present these assets are limited to (1) gold; (2) convertible currencies such as U.S. dollars and sterling, and deposits in such currencies; (3) treasury bills and other obligations issued by the U.S. government. The amendment proposed is a very simple one. It would add one further item to this list, specifically "securities of the international monetary fund maturing not later than five years from the date of issue". This amendment is needed so that Canada can participate in the arrangements for the provision of supplementary resources for the international monetary fund, known as the "fund decision on general arrangements to borrow".
Hon. members may recall that on January 8, 1962, the minister of finance at the time announced that, subject to parliamentary approval, Canada would join nine other leading industrial countries in undertaking to provide stand-by credits to the international monetary fund up to specified amounts. These credits, if and as required, would provide the fund with supplementary resources to support the reserves and balance of payments of one or more of the participating countries if they came under special pressure; in other words, to avoid exchange crises in the participating countries. The agreed purpose is "to forestall or cope with an impairment of the international monetary system".
The ten participants in this arrangement are Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States. Switzerland, although not a member of the fund, is also expected to participate. All the other nine


countries have already adhered formally to the arrangement. Total pledges of support by the ten participants under these arrangements amount to the equivalent of $6 billion in terms of United States currency. The maximum which Canada might be asked to lend under these arrangements would be the equivalent of U.S. $200 million or Canadian $216,216,000 at our current fixed rate of exchange.
Such loans, of course, would not be a budgetary charge. It is anticipated that loans which might be made available by Canada under these arrangements could involve the use of existing resources in the exchange fund account and would consequently not necessarily require net additional Canadian dollar borrowing by the government.
If a participating country makes a loan to the fund under these arrangements it may receive, upon request, securities of the fund equal to the amount of the loan, and bearing interest to maturity based on a formula which at present yields a rate of 1J per cent per annum. The maturity of any such security will not exceed a maximum of five years. The agreed interest rate corresponds approximately to the average rate earned at present by the fund. If the scale of charges made by the fund on its various forms of accommodation were increased, the rate payable to countries providing special resources would be increased accordingly. The fund will also pay a transfer charge of one half of one per cent on each borrowing transaction.
The amendment proposed will provide the legislative authority to allow the exchange fund to invest in securities to be issued by the international monetary fund. Since the purpose of such an investment would be to promote stability in exchange markets, and since any participating country may recall its investment if it experiences balance of payments difficulties, it is appropriate that any supplementary resources called for by the I.M.F. from Canada should be provided through the exchange fund.
The procedures which the ten participants will apply in making supplementary resources available have been embodied in an exchange of letters between the French minister of finance and each of the nine other ministers. On January 8, 1962 the text of the exchange of letters was released by the then minister of finance. In brief, the arrangements would be brought into play on the initiative and under the guidance of the managing director of the international monetary fund. In the very unlikely event that agreement could not be reached among the lending countries regarding their relative shares in any particular transaction, an arrangement for a formal voting procedure is provided.

Canada, because of its dependence on trade, played an important role in the founding of the international monetary fund. Canada was one of the sponsors of the general increase in quotas four years ago, and in fact accepted an increase in its own quota greater than the average.
We are also, as hon. members know, participating currently in international discussions relating to the working of the international financial system. I am sure hon. members will agree that Canada should continue to play a constructive part by participating in the special arrangements now proposed to enable the fund to carry out its growing responsibilities.
In addition to the amendment just outlined, the government proposes another of a purely technical character. This relates to section 22 of the act. This amendment would make it clear that the proceeds upon maturity of securities held by the exchange fund, as well as the proceeds resulting from the sale of such securities, are to be credited to the exchange fund. This amendment is really required because of an oversight in the original legislation; however, it is currently important because securities to be issued by the international monetary fund will be nonnegotiable and hence will be held to maturity if they are not called by the fund for repayment.

maintopic: CURRENCY, MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AUTHORIZATION TO PURCHASE SECURITIES OF INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND
speechtext:
I am sure the committee has listened with interest to the statement which has just been made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance. As he has pointed out, the primary purpose of this legislation concerns a matter which has been under discussion for a substantial period of time. The letters embodying the conditions under which it is proposed to operate were tabled by my predecessor in January, 1962, I think the hon. gentleman said.
I believe legislation along these lines is desirable because it will serve a valuable purpose. This proposal is the legislative culmination of a series of discussions which have been going on over a period of months, if not years, and I hope the committee will see its way clear to adopt the resolution without undue delay, though it is not, of course, for me to say what discussion there should be on it.
As for the second part of the proposal, it is of a purely technical nature necessary to clear up one phase of the operation as far as we are concerned, and I am sure it will commend itself to the committee.

maintopic: CURRENCY, MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AUTHORIZATION TO PURCHASE SECURITIES OF INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND
speechtext:
I do not propose to hold up the committee for very long. I just want to make some comments on this subject because I have brought this question before the house on a
Mint and Exchange Fund Act number of occasions. I refer to the difficulties in which the world is getting in regard to international trade.
In spite of the reply given by the Minister of Finance to a question I put to him, I am unable to place any other interpretation upon this bill than that it is a stopgap proposal, or a small, faltering step toward a final solution of the problems of international trade. It is significant that the ten countries which are at present engaged in negotiations in Paris should be the same ten countries which are involved in this proposal. There have been repeated news reports both from Europe and the United States about 'the Paris discussions, and there have been a number of plans put forward for improving the situation with regard to international liquidity. One of them was referred to recently in the New York Times, the Bernstein plan; and there is another which is perhaps more far reaching in its implications and which has also been discussed.
I hope Canada will not be among the countries which will drag their feet when it comes to moving more rapidly toward a final solution of these difficulties. There will certainly be opposition to any radical changes. Some of these objections were voiced by the new director of the international monetary fund shortly after he took office. Not long afterwards, though, he beat a retreat and suggested that while in his opinion there was no present serious shortage of international exchange, such a situation might arise and it would therefore be as well to proceed with investigations.
I hope we will not stop at investigations. This is reminiscent of the days some 30 years ago when national economies were trying to free themselves from the restrictions of the gold standard. The same sort of objections were raised then to any departure from the gold standard that are being raised today against more revolutionary proposals for an international unit of exchange. I hope the Canadian government, through its delegation, will be among those who will be pressing for the exploration of every possible means by which the world economic community can move into the position which is now occupied by national economic units in relation to the exchange medium.

maintopic: CURRENCY, MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AUTHORIZATION TO PURCHASE SECURITIES OF INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND
speechtext:
The principle involved in this resolution is of vital concern to us. As we were in extreme difficulties during the thirties, when the gold basis of our national monetary unit was proving unsatisfactory, so are we today in difficulty on the international scene as far as the gold standard is concerned. However, following the principles we have enunciated when speaking about reform as far as the operation of the rules

Mint and Exchange Fund Act in this house are concerned, we are content to let this resolution pass now and take the opportunity of examining the serious aspects which are involved in this proposal when it comes before us as legislation.
We find this measure brought before us on exactly the same day that press reports have come out regarding plans for a global currency system now under consideration by ten nations. We find that these are the same ten nations involved in this particular resolution. This situation causes us to wonder. I wonder, myself, why Switzerland is not in this arrangement. However, there will be an opportunity to debate and discuss this matter fully when it comes before us as legislation, and we shall deal with it more specifically on that occasion.

maintopic: CURRENCY, MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AUTHORIZATION TO PURCHASE SECURITIES OF INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe the few questions I had the opportunity to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) today during the question period succeeded in opening the eyes of some of the other members of this house to the results of this resolution which appears as item 14 on the order paper.
In my opinion, were it only a matter of studying the resolution in itself and in a general way, there would probably be no problem.
The question is simply to establish a reserve fund for the various countries so that, should one of the ten countries-Canada, France or the United States-find itself in difficulties in respect of its foreign exchange reserve to deal with the others, that ten-country club, known as the Paris club, would lend money to that country, so that it would find it easier to carry out its transactions.
We must not forget one thing, however. This famous Paris club has ten members, practically all countries belonging to the common market except Luxembourg, Great Britain, Canada, the United States and Japan.
Those discussions were followed by a second stage where efforts were made to set up an international currency. This is where we raise objections. History proves that there was at the first stage, a chain reaction which is difficult to stop.
The next step will be the establishment of an international currency, as the New York Times stated recently. That scares us a little, Mr. Chairman. Why? Because Canada, like the nine other members of the Paris club, does not control its own currency.
Our monetary unit, at 92.5 per cent, that is credit, and we do not even control it.
[Mr. Thompson-'!
And now countries which do not even control their monetary unit will agree to create a monetary unit that will be under whose control then?
The danger lies there. If you consider those ten countries that make up the Paris club and if you consider which ones control their credit, you will find that control vested in four or five international credit trusts: Kuhn and Loeb, J. P. Morgan, the Rothschilds, the Lazares. Here is where it all ends: four international financial trusts, and London's Barclay's Bank.
I can see the Minister of Finance seems to find it funny that trusts such as these should be mentioned. But, Mr. Chairman, let us not forget that when, for instance, the Imperial Bank of Canada and the Canadian Bank of Commerce merged-two of our most important chartered banks-to form one of the largest banks which controls money and credit in this country, and when that merger was announced in the official Canada Gazette, it was seen in the last paragraph that those two banks were controlled by the Barclay's Bank of London.
Now, if we take a look at all our chartered banks, if we examine the situation of the banks controlled in the United States, in France, in Italy, in the Netherlands, in Belgium, in Japan, in West Germany, we find that the same four big international financial trusts I mentioned a while ago control credit and the growth of credit in each of those countries.
And as a first step, which may seem very normal-it seems to be a procedure designed for mutual help-those ten countries propose: "That loans be made or at least securities issued on the market, which will be meant to guarantee us against the difficulties one of the ten countries might have." But who will control the securities and the $200 million worth of securities issued at the start by Canada, to be deposited if need be-not immediately if there is no immediate need, but if needed-in this new monetary fund?
Mind you the terms used are, as I can see it, rather ambiguous-they do not tell the truth; they say "securities of the international monetary fund". It is not a matter of putting moneys in some international monetary fund or a matter of doing business with the international monetary fund, it is a fund which is entirely distinct from the international monetary fund; the one we are now being asked to approve would be just a fund available to those ten countries.
We are afraid of that step, Mr. Chairman. While, today, Canada is the only country in the ten member Paris club which has signed the agreement to which parliament has not yet affixed its signature and about which it

has not as yet made up its mind-it is assumed that Canada will follow, as usual, England, the United States and the other countries, it is assumed that Canada will always follow in their wake-we are presented with the second stage, which is the creation of an international unit for the ten countries included in the Paris club, whose international units and control lie precisely with the same four financial cartels.
Mr. Chairman, the reason given is that the countries can be in need of this and may meet with difficulties in the field of international trade. Well, as far as this is concerned, I shall tell the Minister of Finance that if Canada, under the present administration as well as under the previous one, experiences or has experienced difficulties, this is not because of the economic situation of Canada during peacetime but because of the mismanagement and wrong monetary system that we now have in Canada.
Instead of attempting first to do things like that, we should rather think of making the necessary changes in our monetary system, in order to be able to anticipate, so that we will not have the difficulties we now experience, like those we had in the past.
The economic situation of Canada might be very sound, but it is badly affected, not because of men or because of the wealth of this country, but because of the monetary and financial system we have in Canada. This is a mistake the Minister of Finance should correct, instead of committing us to another system of international control by financial trusts.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that this resolution should have been much more carefully scrutinized, so that we could have roused public opinion on the venture in which the government intends to launch us at this time.
However, we will accept the resolution in order to see at least, how far the bill can lead us. But the government will have to guarantee that Canada will not join this famous Paris club, a club of ten countries all "controlled" by international finance trusts.
When the bill is before us, we will be in a better position to discuss it, because we will then know what it is all about. However, I wish to warn the Minister of Finance right now that with all the latest developments we can open our eyes and foresee where this first stage of the Paris club of ten is leading us.

There are natural seaports such as the one to be found in Halifax or Vancouver. But Montreal has a harbour which is the gateway not only to the sea but to several inland provinces. I suggest the government should submit the matter to the committee.
The question is an important one. The former minister of transport, Mr. Hees, had given some thought to Montreal harbour becoming a winter port. I hope the minister will make it a point to suggest to the committee to hear witnesses who will no doubt have some interesting things to say on that matter.
Moreover, some time ago, the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec complained about an important decline in maritime traffic due to the fact that they did not participate to a sufficient extent in the administration of the national harbours board's business.
I do not know if that matter falls under the jurisdiction of the committee itself, but I take this opportunity to point out to the minister the representations made in that respect as well as the requests made by the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec to have more say in the administration of the Montreal harbour.
Mr. Speaker, there are many other questions I could deal with now, but just now, I hope that the minister will take steps to ensure that the committee will consider also the whole question concerning the water and highway transport system in Canada.
For many years already, national organizations have urged the Minister of Transport to revise its entire maritime policy and I hope that we shall have the opportunity, as we sit on the committee, to examine those questions in the light of experts' knowledge as well as of the suggestions that will be made by the members of parliament.

The shock we had when the hon. member for Ottawa West was made Minister of Transport was really not shock at any question of his ability or competence to take over such an important field where the burden of administration and the need for policy decision are so great, as that someone should have been chosen who had taken so little interest and who had followed, from all I can find out in the parliamentary record, almost no avenue in the transport field at all.
I consider that this is the most important of the administrative departments of government. I think in many ways it is the most difficult one. I cannot, like hon. gentlemen to my right, postulate a golden age when Mr. Hees or the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) was in charge of the department. I do not feel it was any golden age. But if I can get back to the period before the war and immediately after, it seems to me our transportation policy did have some purpose even if it wound up being debilitated by royal commissions which never really came to any decisions.
In recent years we have had a long public debate on transport issues. I disagree with many of the recommendations of the MacPherson commission but I am prepared to admit, and my colleagues in the main are prepared to admit, that many of the recommendations of that commission are acceptable at the present time despite the fact that the previous government claimed it had legislation; that this legislation was ready; that it had been worked out in consultation with

Railways, Air Lines and Shipping various groups including Mr. Gordon and Mr. Crump and with all the associations involved. The fact remains that this government was elected in April; here we are in November, and last week it was indicated by the Prime Minister that we would have to wait a good bit longer still. I think this is as unsatisfactory as the fact that this week we shall be examining the two annual reports of these crown corporations while at the same time there is another almost due.
I want to make some comments about the reappointment of Mr. Gordon. Mr. Gordon told us last year that he was born in December, 1901, and I think those of us who have had any contact with him are quite aware that he seems to be a healthy man. There is no evidence of approaching senility. He is a very vigorous person, and he still seems quite able to state his views and his ideas very positively.

That is just size. Mr. Gordon has been reappointed with a time limit placed upon the appointment. I assume this is a bargain that has been struck because of differences within the Liberal party and the government, and I can sympathize with their differences because I know that somewhat the same differences existed in the previous administration with regard to Mr. Gordon. But the point is that if the 18 months limitation means anything, Mr. Gordon will be retiring before he reaches the normal retirement age of 65, and it would certainly seem to me that it would be a retirement before he had exhausted his capacity for service.
Personally I am delighted that the Canadian National is going to see the end of Mr. Gordon in 16 months from now or 18 months from the date of his reappointment, but I do feel that in this period the government should be giving a great deal of consideration to whom his successor is going to be. I suggest that a considerable amount of care needs to be taken in the selection, and I think it is worth while suggesting to the minister that the appointment should not be a political one in any way, and that whoever is appointed it should not be someone who is committed at the present time either to one side or the other in the whole matter of labour and management; because one of the great challenges of the next president of the C.N.R. is the whole matter of relations with labour within the company. There will need to be a tremendous effort to uplift the morale of the employees and get better co-operation from the workers of the railway than Mr. Gordon has been able to achieve.


I think the matter requires a great deal of consideration, and I mention it because I have been shocked, and I hope many other members of parliament have been shocked, by the rather loose speculation that the present Minister of Justice is being considered as a potential president of Canadian National Railways. I can think of nothing that would serve to accelerate the destruction of Canadian National Railways more than such an appointment. I do not say this in order to make fun of the Minister of Justice. It is just the fact that neither his background in transport nor his political connections are the kind of thing that we want in the man heading this important crown corporation.
The main criticism we have had of the operations of Canadian National Railways in recent years has centred on the fact that despite the tremendous amount of money that has been poured into the railway by the taxpayers, the debt of the railway has gone up somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1,600 million. I believe the annual interest burden has gone up from around $120 million a year to approximately $380 million a year.
Throughout his regime as president Mr. Gordon's argument has always tended to be twofold. If the structure of Canadian National Railways could be modernized, then it would become a going concern and he would be able to show lots of black ink in the books. If hon. members will look at the last page of the C.N.R. annual report, where there is a 25 year synoptical history of Canadian National Railways, they will see that in the period of Gordon's presidency there have been only four years when the railway was not in the red, and in recent years the annual deficit has been substantial. I have been somewhat amused by the fact that in the part of the 1961 report, for example, under the heading "The Outlook" there is this sentence:
The 1961 financial result was a cause erf deep concern to the board of directors and the management. Over the past several years, despite the most resolute and intense efforts, Canadian National operations have resulted in successive and substantial annual deficits.
Then it goes on to say:
There are, however, some hopeful signs which could lead to an opportunity for the system to bring a break-even position within its reach.
Then we go to the 1962 report and we find the following:
The foregoing report records improvements, additions and service changes to C.N.'s complex plant and facilities. It is significant to note, as well, that the new form of administrative organization, now in its third year, has contributed to the improved sales showing and is considered to have brought a new spirit of enthusiasm throughout the system. The organizational structure, which emphasizes local responsibility, is producing more flexible operations tailored to customer demand. The board of directors

and management, however, feel that the true impact of the accomplishments of 1962 and prior years, which produced a major rehabilitation of the property, is obscured by the heavy burden of long term debt. There is a marked divergence between what might be termed the "service result" and the "bookkeeping result".
In other words, what Mr. Gordon has been trying to tell us is that we have a good, going operation from a service and equipment point of view, but that it is never going to look worth a darn unless the railway can get the huge annual interest burden and the big debt off the books. Here again it would be interesting to hear from the minister-I hope before the committee-what he plans to do in this regard. After all, I believe it is 18 months since Mr. Gordon made his presentation to the ministry in regard to this very question.
When Mr. Gordon is not blaming the heavy debt structure for the poor annual operating picture in terms of revenue he is blaming those hungry people, the railway workers, and saying that any gains that are obtained by Canadian National Railways are chewed up by the insatiable demands of the workers when they enter into contract negotiations. It is worth reflecting that right at the moment Canadian National Railways, like Canadian Pacific Railway, has before it demands from almost all the unions that have contracts with management, and these demands are again going to be of considerable size in terms of both wages and fringe benefits. I think these are necessary demands, because in my view they reflect the needs of the railway workers to keep up with increases both in wages and in fringe benefits in other areas. Just because railway workers are scattered across the country in so many communities I think they should be the bell-weather of our whole labour force and its wage rates.
But the excuse of heavy debt and the excuse of the insatiable demands of labour have never really been met, it seems to me, by Mr. Gordon in his presidency. It seems to me the reason is that Mr. Gordon has never really been able to make up his mind what he wants to do with Canadian National Railways. I insist that the Achilles heel of Canadian National Railways has simply been the fact that Mr. Gordon has played around the idea that if he only had the money to invest he could have a money maker, and the fact that we as politicians and the country as a whole make demands upon the Canadian National transportation system that defy and go against the whole opportunity of having that kind of enterprise. We see other examples of this. Right now, my colleagues from Winnipeg are raising cain over the movement of the T.C.A. depot to Montreal. Hon.
Railways, Air Lines and Shipping members from Montreal are getting up and suggesting the government ought to saddle T.C.A. with what I think is, in modern times, an archaic aircraft, the Caravelle.
However, these things are done, and the intentions of hon. members are of the best in terms of their own area and the objectives they want to achieve. Well, you could multiply examples like those on the railroads, particularly the Canadian National Railways, a dozen times. I have always felt that every hon. member who took an interest in railroading should read Colonel Stevens two-volume work on the Canadian National and how it developed out of the Grand Trunk and the Intercolonial. They would see so many examples contradicting the possibility of operating the Canadian National Railways as the kind of free enterprise of which Mr. Gordon dreamed, showing black on the books.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, I think the fundamental mistake of Mr. Gordon has been to kid himself and to kid the country that it will be possible to achieve this kind of operation. One of the interesting things that happened when these two corporations were before this committee last year, was the evidence of Mr. McGregor, the president of T.C.A. He was being pressed with regard to the financial picture of T.C.A., which last year was not good. He was explaining that T.C.A., unlike C.P.A., was carrying a whole bunch of what he called social routes, and came up with this particular answer about social routes:
I do not know whether C.P.A. will move into the black in 1963. X know Mr. McConachie said so, but I also know that he has said the same thing about other years when he did not move into the black.
T.C.A. however could move into the black in 1963, with the rider, however, which is most important, that there will be no further encroachments on our traffic position. There are three or four routes now under application by C.P.A., so X would like to stress the absolute need for the rider that our calculation concerning the 1963 operating position is based entirely on no worsening of our competitive position.
Now, about the social routes, so-called, many of these are operated by T.C.A.
One can think of a number of them, such as Windsor to London, Vancouver to Victoria and some of the maritime lines. Then, Mr. McGregor goes on:
Whether or not they move them from black to red is really of no great importance. If the company is black with the social routes, then it would have been blacker without them. Without the social routes the ability of the company to reduce fares would have been greater than would be the case if the social routes are depressing net revenues.
I have recognized that many of these social routes
have to be operated in some way or other________a
place cannot just be thrown to the wolves so far as air transport is concerned, simply because it does not have the ability to generate enough air traffic to keep a line alive, particularly if it is in a remote area or across water, or something of that

Railways, Air Lines and Shipping nature-I think it must be recognized that social routes as such, as long as they are operated are a drain on the finances of the company. However if the finances of the profitable routes are such that they can support those social routes, and still not go into the red, probably everybody is happy.
This was the contribution Mr. McGregor made in pointing out that T.C.A. carries the burden of these so-called social routes from its more prosperous routes on which the jets and Vanguards fly. This particular principle has really never been to the fore in the thinking of Mr. Gordon about Canadian National Railways. He has always had his eye on the goal that some day, probably like Sir Henry Thornton or Mr. Crump or Sir Edward Beatty, he would be able to show a consistently black balance at the end of every year. Then, he would be able to feel he had proven that a government enterprise, in the competitive field, could do the job. I do not think it is possible, after looking at his record over these years, for this to be done. I would hope that in considering the next president of Canadian National Railways the government would consider that we need a president like Mr. McGregor who is willing to accept and put forward the possibility of carrying, if you will, social routes, the non-competitive part of the system, because this is part of national transportation policy.
It has always seemed to me that Mr. Gordon has been in conflict with this generally accepted idea in this country, the idea that the balance sheet is really not as important as the service that is supplied to the people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, one of the things I wanted to comment upon in connection with the Canadian National Railways is the position Mr. Gordon put the railway into with his appearance before the committee last year. I was sitting in the committee, and I could see what was coming when he shrugged off one of his assistants and made that answer to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) that led to the fuss and furore over French Canadians who worked for Canadian National Railways, and the fact that none of the top executive positions in the company was held by a French Canadian. It seems to me that in this particular discussion, both those who felt Mr. Gordon was justified and those who were critical, would be well advised to draw away from the matter and leave it alone for a while.
I suggest this for two reasons. First, it seems to me there is an indication of some new efforts on the part of Canadian National in this regard. They are going to do their best to meet the requests and demands of the French Canadians to have better representation in the system at all levels. Second, if these people do not leave the subject alone I

fear that there will be, within the personnel of the railway, an extremely strong reaction, particularly in that portion of the Canadian National which operates in a part of the country remote from large groups of French Canadians. I put this idea forward to my colleagues in the house, rather than to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith).
I find that Mr. Gordon's popularity with the majority of Canadian National workers has never been extremely high, but that it has improved markedly as he has been under pressure over this matter of employing and advancing French Canadians in the railway. I would hope that both the president and the railway would have an opportunity over the next year or two to show their good faith without the consistent harping pressure, for example, based upon whether a conductor's hat is lettered in French words or English words.
One of the other points in connection with Canadian National Railways has been touched upon by the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade), and that is the trucking operation of Canadian National Railways. One of the anomalies, it seems to me, of the recommendations of the MacPherson royal commission is the emphasis on competitive modes of transport. The essence of the MacPherson recommendations is that there should be intense competition between competing modes of transport. Nobody has really looked at the point, Mr. Speaker, that both the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railways have competition in all the modes except, I suppose, pipe lines and passenger automobiles. If the object is real competition between the modes, then it surely seems to me that when monopoly ownership jumps from one mode to the other, that is the real danger to any fruition of the competitive principle.
Mr. Gordon was broached on this last year before the committee, and to me his statement just did not make sense. This is a quotation from page 54 of the committee proceedings where I had been questioning him. He said:
I will put it this way. In every mode of transport that we can see as being feasible to use for the purpose of handling traffic and to give our shippers service, and in respect of which we can make some money, certainly we will use anything.
I asked him:
Do you see any conflict at all between the transportation policy that emphasizes competition and the role that you play in providing a public service in an area which is not now and likely never will be on a competing basis?
Mr. Gordon said:
I do not see anything wrong with that. The commission says quite definitely-and I am speaking from memory-that the railways will not be and should not be expected in the future to provide any services which would mean that they lose money on it; but they go on to say that if

there is any, whatever the service may be which the board of transport commissioners finds on examination is required in the public interest, then that service should be continued by the railways and should be paid for by supplementary subsidies. So, the commission is perfectly consistent in saying that the railways should not provide any transportation that loses money. I repeat that if a particular service is regarded as being in the public interest, then the commission says flatly that the railways should be compensated for their losses.
I do not say he did it deliberately, but in effect Mr. Gordon evaded the point, that if you are going to have competing modes of transportation how does it bear with both major railways in the country, involved in the major modes of transportation? How can you have genuine competition unless you look forward to the extension of these giants, particularly in trucking, 50 per cent owned by C.P. and 50 per cent by C.N.? That is the direction in which truck ownership is moving, and that is why a lot of trucking people are worried.
The royal commission suggested that trucking is such an easy mode to enter, that the amount of capital required is so little, that there will always be a truly competitive factor there. I do not think this is so, because I do not think the capital requirements are that small. In fact it seems to me they are increasing. But even more, what is required in trucking is the obtaining of a franchise and the control of a franchise.
Not one of the provinces at the present time is opening up any of these franchises, and there are a great lot of interceders when there is a franchise. In other words, it is not wide open, and it is exactly there where the C.N.R. and C.P.R. are bringing to bear the pressure of their immense capital resources to obtain routes, and also the legal services they have to appear before provincial boards, such as the one in Quebec, in order to extend their operations.
I suggest there is a real conflict here between the recommendations of the MacPher-son report on competition, particularly since we are involved in this as politicians, and the extension and permeation of the trucking business by the C.N.R. This is something we need to examine quite closely when we look at the operations of the C.N.R. in the committee.
There is one other point I want to touch on in connection with Canadian National Railways problems. There is a tendency, because of the abruptness and directness with which Mr. Gordon speaks, that when he comes out with a major pronouncement it gains considerable approval, particularly in our business press, and the critical reaction that follows is usually slow and not nearly as effective.

One of the things Mr. Gordon did over a year ago was to go into western Canada and make a speech about the handling of wheat in western Canada. He suggested Canada was 50 years behind the times, and we needed to revert to a master plan. He outlined how that master plan would work, and ever since then the prairies have been kicking; but I do not think they have really caught up with the masterful case that sounded so simple and attractive when Mr. Gordon put it forward. For that reason I want to put on the record some comments from the northwest line elevators association in criticism of this master plan. I think this points out some of the reasons we need a master transportation policy that is controlled and directed by someone in the federal government.
I had this letter in December last from Mr. Lamont, president of the northwest line elevators association in which he says:
Mr. Donald Gordon, president of Canadian National Railways, recently appeared before the House of Commons committee on railways and during the course of his examination Mr. Gordon made certain statements relating to the grain elevator handling system of western Canada. His statements before the committee were along the lines of a recent address made by him before the Canadian club of Winnipeg on the same subject, copy of which we have read.
We do not feel that Mr. Gordon's statements were made in the light of informed knowledge of what has actually taken place in the elevator trade of western Canada.
In other words, Mr. Gordon did not know what he was talking about.
For this reason we have written to Mr. Gordon and we enclose for your information, copy of the letter directed to him under date of December 7.
I have that letter here, and I just want to make the point that the letter contains a number of quotations from Mr. Gordon's remarks. Here is one of his remarks:
The system of grain handling established before the first world war-the collection, storage and transport of the prairie crop-has changed very little.
Here is another:
Many of the existing country elevators are now well below the optimum size for the best economic costs of operation and also for the most economic cost of transshipment by railways.
Here is another quotation:
The second factor involves the economies that can be obtained through a program of elevator consolidation that would eliminate those existing elevators that are operating well below the size required to ensure the lowest cost operation.
Another one is:
Elevator consolidation on main lines would enable the railway to pick up more cars at one time and reduce transportation and switching costs.

Railways, Air Lines and Shipping Then the letter continues:
The press report of your appearance before the railways committee said that Mr. Gordon was expanding on suggestions on grain handling he made in a speech to the Winnipeg Canadian club in September.
Then the association goes on to point out its experience in the grain business. It says they have been in operation since 1899 and have had a considerable share in this elevator traffic. Now I want to put down some of the points they concluded with, in connection with Mr. Gordon's suggestions. They said:
Would your proposed system of main line "master elevators" serve the farmer more efficiently and at less cost than existing elevators?
We feel sure that this would not be the case for the following reasons:
1.	The farmer would have to haul his grain longer distances to market and every additional mile brings added costs in gasoline, wear and tear on trucks and man-hours consumed going to and from the elevators.
2.	If the farmer, through branch line abandonment, was forced to haul his grain double the existing average 10 mile haul to market, it would cost him an additional five cents per bushel to market his grain. This would be equivalent to a freight rate increase of 42 per cent based on present average freight costs of 12 cents per bushel.
3.	You do not make it clear under your plan whether the government or the railways propose to compensate the farmer for the additional haulage costs. If you do not, then you are in effect increasing the farmer's freight costs by 42 per cent. If you do, then the cost would have to be borne by the taxpayer and as a taxpayer the farmer would participate in these added costs.
These sound like pretty good arguments to me.
4.	The farmer would be faced with long waits for his turn to unload his truck at the "master elevator". This could only be overcome by building plants that would be equivalent in most aspects to a terminal plant except in size, and the costly nature of the workhouses would not be compensated as at terminal points, through spreading it over large capacity.
5.	Under existing conditions of elevator operation, the country elevator agent assumes the capacity of local manager and in periods of heavy deliveries operates his elevator for long hours to serve his customers. At a central "master elevator", located many miles from the farm, the manager-customer relationship would be lost. Hours of delivery would have to be regulated or two or three shifts would have to be engaged, all of which would add to the cost of handling grain.
6.	Grain elevator storage charges today are the same rate as they were in 1912. Elevation charges on wheat have increased only one and one quarter cents per bushel compared with 1912, with similar percentage increases for other grains. We do not know of any other non-subsidized industry with such a record for holding down its charges. These charges could not be maintained under your plan.
Then the last two points deal with the fact that royal commissions have investigated grain handling in Canada many times since 1899:
Invariably they have commended the efficiency of Canada's grain handling methods. Where improvements have been recommended, they have been adopted.

Point 8 is this:
You have dealt too lightly with the time-consuming factor whereby the farmer, under your scheme, would have to spend much more of his time delivering grain. During the farming season the farmer's time resources are pressed to the utmost. The fact is that the labour situation is such in the large farm units of today that there is no spare help, and the farmer's own time is fully occupied.
That pretty well concludes the main arguments against this master plan of grain delivery. I wanted to put this on the record, not because I am tremendously interested in this problem-because I do not represent a prairie constituency-but the Gordon approach here is identical with the Gordon approach with regard to the changes that have been made on the railway in spending this tremendous sum of money for dieselization, central traffic control, all these master agency schemes and the new build-up of the organization where he is decentralized and has chiefs all over the place. The Indians on the railway are disappearing very quickly, but we are getting a great many more chiefs. The whole burden of Mr. Gordon's arguments throughout all this change is that he is going to create a more efficient railway and cut down costs. I suggest that he has had 12 years to prove what he can do, 12 clear years, and yet look at the situation in terms of the debt and interest charges of Canadian National Railways. In the process, this kind of approach manages to damn the man who works on the railway; he wants too much; he is inflexible; there are too many unions; they are not co-operative enough; they get in management's way. I suppose that in so far as this master plan of grain delivery is concerned, it is the farmers in the west who are the nuts and obstructionists now.
In other words, I am trying to suggest that in Mr. Gordon you have an able, hard working, even overbearing president who has been charging down various lines to create an efficient operation almost on the perfect free enterprise or private enterprise model. He has mistaken the real purpose of what the Canadian people want out of their government-owned railway. Railways, Air Lines and Shipping

maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OP COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been listening this afternoon to a very interesting and wide ranging debate on this resolution to set up a sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping. This was, of course, to be expected because of the great complex of these public utilities under the control of the federal government. Their very existence under this control is meant to ensure that our far flung land and water areas can be knit together to form a cohesive whole. The value of binding the nation together with a modern transportation system I believe cannot be estimated in dollars alone. Unwillingness on our part to accept this fact could spell disaster for our country.
With this in mind I should like to discuss briefly with the committee this afternoon two single items now confronting our transportation system. The first is in connection with the proposed removal of the T.C.A. repair and maintenance depot from Winnipeg. The second is the matter of railway branch line abandonment. With regard to the removal of repair depots, there is always the danger under our federal system of a trend toward greater centralization. It is true this may make it easier for administrative purposes and it may even, in some circumstances, result in lower costs. However, the fact that Winnipeg lies on the trans-polar route would indicate that perhaps in the not too distant future that city will become one of the important air links in North American transportation.
The Winnipeg Free Press of June 19, 1963 had this to say:
There are powerful arguments for the retention of the base in Winnipeg. Montreal is the air line's centre for servicing long-distance jets. The suggestion of the (Manitoba) delegation is that Winnipeg's base be converted to take care of the overhaul and maintenance of smaller, domestic jet aircraft which will replace the Viscount and Vanguard aircraft now in use; the base ought to be capable of taking care of larger aircraft as well.
Furthermore, the removal of the base would be contrary to the national interest in respect to national defence and civil emergency policy.
If this trend toward centralization is to continue-and it is a trend which, because of defence and other considerations is highly undesirable-we may end up with two or three super cities gathering the industries of the country together to the detriment of the whole economy. I am not proposing that the question of the repair and maintenance base be studied by the committee as yet, because all Manitoba members expect the minister to announce his decision in this regard very shortly. They hope for a favourable decision, and their optimism is based on the remarks of the Liberal candidate for Winnipeg South Centre in the last election when, referring
Railways, Air Lines and Shipping to a telegram he had received from the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) he said: "This ensures that the T.C.A. maintenance and overhaul base will continue in Winnipeg". I realize the Prime Minister has denied he made any commitment in this regard, but the right hon. gentleman has said, as reported in the Winnipeg Tribune of May 21, that his party is committed to a policy of decentralized regional industrial and economic development. This policy should be a major consideration in reaching any decision on the T.C.A. base.
The second matter I should like to bring to the attention of the committee concerns branch railway line abandonment. Until such time as a complete analysis has been made of the prairie region and until a national transportation policy has been established to take into account the social as well as the economic needs of our people, it seems to me that any further abandonment of railway branch lines does not make good sense. This is particularly true since we have made these huge wheat sales to the communist countries. There is every indication that such sales will continue, at least into the foreseeable future. The decision of the former government to suspend applications for railway line abandonment opens the way for a more careful study by this government of this complex problem, should it choose to undertake such a study. The Manitoba Co-operator for January 10, 1963 had the following to say in this regard:
The decision reached at the high level meeting in Ottawa January 4, with the railways suspending applications to abandon branch lines in western Canada, is a good one. It paves the way for a knowledgeable and sensible solution to the problem of rail line abandonment.
Another article which appeared in the same newspaper on September 5, had this to say:
The approach to individual line abandonment must be made with extreme caution. A railway line is part of the economic and social fabric of an area, and the decision as to whether it goes or stays will have far reaching effects on the people of that area. At the same time, every branch line is a part of our over-all national transportation system which will be affected every time a line is abandoned. Because of this, and because of the many factors to be taken into consideration in planning a sound national transportation system, a broadly-based railway rationalization board is necessary.
The MacPherson royal commission stressed the need for co-operation between the railway companies, railway labour and the shipping industry in the creation and discharge of a transportation program, but it does not provide for the co-ordination of a program of line abandonment and grain handling consolidation. It urges that an agency of the board of grain commissioners, or another body named by the government, be made

Railways, Air Lines and Shipping responsible for the planning and control of a program designed to consolidate the existing grain storage and handling capacity so as to provide a more economic and better system in conjunction with possible changes in rail transportation. The commission was not required to deal in any detail with the problems presented by rail line abandonment, and it did not do so. But I think this leaves the western farmers wondering what is likely to happen to them as far as their future is concerned. Under the commission's findings the farmers could haul as far as 25 miles economically to an existing line. If this happens they agreed that perhaps up to 9,000 miles of prairie rail line could be abandoned. Take anything like 9,000 miles of branch line out of the prairie provinces and consider the number of towns and villages along those lines which would face economic disaster. I think careful consideration should be given before rail line abandonment is made on any large scale. The Prime Minister, speaking in Selkirk, Manitoba, on March 8, said that if elected a Liberal government would establish a committee of inquiry to investigate the effects of railway branch line abandonments. He added:
The committee's report will he the foundation of a railway policy based on the best interest of all concerned groups and designed to maintain essential branch line services.

I think we all agree that the entire question of consumer credit needs very serious review and that we should go to the very basis of the subject matter, as this committee will be able to do.
One of the defects of this particular bill, Mr. Speaker, is that possibly it has not been gone into in sufficient detail, particularly with regard to its constitutional aspect. I do not think we can possibly resolve the very deep-seated problems which affect credit generally in this country, and consumer credit in particular, without considering them in relationship to the constitution of the country. Unfortunately, at this level of government we have under our constitution, jurisdiction over interest pursuant to the British North America Act, but we do not have jurisdiction over private property and civil rights. Pursuant to the constitution that matter falls within provincial jurisdiction.
I do not think that this problem can be solved at either one level or the other. If we approach it from the provincial viewpoint of private property and civil rights, I think we inevitably run afoul of the federal powers under the constitution which give control of interest to the federal government. On the other hand, I do not think that in approaching this problem purely by virtue of the powers of the federal government over interest, as does this bill so attempt, we arrive at a full solution to the problem either. I think there is no doubt that this is one of the very fundamental matters which has belaboured us in this house, particularly in past years and certainly in this session. I am referring to those things which we may do here within the constitution and which we deem necessary for the welfare of our people, and those things that are necessary for the welfare of our people which may not be done either constitutionally or under some new concept which has now come into being in our federalism and in our constitution. Even though it is constitutionally proper for the federal government to do certain things, by reason of this new concept, they can only be done with the approbation of the provinces, although these things are within the federal sphere under the constitution. This shows how difficult it is to legislate in these matters.
I think all of us were very pleased to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) say the other day in no uncertain and in very positive terms, paraphrasing Sir Winston Churchill, that he had not come to this house to see the liquidation of the Canadian constitution. These were indeed reassuring words, especially as we have heard so much in the
