house, since parliament convened in April, about provincial rights, parochial rights, municipal rights, but so little about Canada, the powers needed federally in order to make Canada a strong land which could forge ahead, and about giving the proper federal powers needed in this very complex world to do the things socially and economically required by our people. It was reassuring for us on this side to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) speak as he did. If there is one thing which binds us together on this side of the house, it is the great part which the Liberal party has played in bringing back to the federal government the powers it needs in order to confront the many problems with which the 20th century presents us. I think that when the constitution was formulated it was intended that the reserve power under the peace, order and good government clause should reside in the federal government. The fathers of confederation were farsighted enough to see that, as economic and social needs grew, the federal government must have the legislative and fiscal power needed to enable it to satisfy these new needs.
Unfortunately, as a result of narrowminded and incompetent judicial decisions by the privy council early in the century, the federal power under the clause to which I have referred was truncated and emasculated, until, if the privy council decisions were to be heeded, residual power was virtually vested in the provinces. I think history will record that the great thing this party has accomplished in its 22 years of office was the recovery of so much of that residuary power. The great place in history of Mackenzie King in particular will result from the fact that, through his wisdom and his understanding of the problems of Canada and its peoples, without creating any great provincial turmoil and, in a large measure, with the approbation of the provinces, he was able to bring Canada back to the position which the fathers of confederation had intended, namely that the residual power, the vast residue of power, should rest with the federal government. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISCLOSURE OF COST OF CREDIT
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. As I stated earlier, while I appreciate the motives of the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill- he is against transactions in connection with which persons are not made fully aware of the rate of interest they have to pay-I submit, with respect, that a fundamental shortcoming of this measure is that he has forgotten about our Canadian constitution. It may be that the constitution will have to be revised in order that the worth-while objectives which the hon. member has in mind may be achieved. If that type of revision should be necessary, I am sure that we on this side would be pleased to support the hon. member in approaching the provinces to that end, should it be the type of amendment, as I imagine it would, where the consent of the provinces was required in order to amend the constitution so as to make legislation of this comprehensive type valid at the federal level. If this is to be done, I would be the first to agree with the hon. member that such a change in the constitution should be made by amending the constitution, not by expedients, or day to day meetings, or discussion with the provinces; not by some nebulous

term such as co-operative federalism. I say it should be done by a clear amendment to the constitution, so as to carry out what the fathers of confederation had intended.
I agree there might be great difficulty about amending the constitution but, if, in 1865 there were men in this land who had sufficient vision-if that is not a nasty word-and sufficient energy, foresight, and courage to draw up the original constitution then, surely, little can be said for us who sit in this house today, if we do not have people of such calibre and sincerity as to achieve our objectives by a forthright amendment to the constitution, rather than leave these wide overlapping areas of jurisdiction. Nobody knows whom these areas belong to. Apparently legislation concerning them should be carried out now, under this new heading of co-operative federalism. Well, there may be a narrow area which would best be left in this nebulous field, but by and large I suggest it would be far better to have government by law, by placing with the federal government the powers it needs to carry out its task and by placing with the provincial governments the powers, both fiscal and legislative, which they need in order to carry out theirs. Governments at both levels would be able to raise the funds they needed and do what they had to do, clearly within the constitution, so that we might continue to have government by law rather than government by men.

maintopic: INTEREST ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISCLOSURE OF COST OF CREDIT
speechtext: I quite agree with what the hon. gentleman has just said, but I would point out to him that interest rates are one of the things that come under federal jurisdiction.

maintopic: INTEREST ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISCLOSURE OF COST OF CREDIT
speechtext:
I concur in what the hon. member says, but may I relate once more to the bill in question what I have said respecting our constitution. May I point out there is a vast area that the hon. member has attempted to leave out of the bill, because he very clearly saw that it was not within the constitutional ambit of the federal gov-ernmen. But I fear that even here he has transgressed on provincial authority by referring in the proposed section 16 (b) in the bill to such things as brokerage fees and charges, bonuses, service charges, subscriptions, dues and premiums. These matters may well come within the area that has been defined judicially as being private property and civil rights, rather than interest, and if such is the case then to that extent his bill would be unconstitutional.
I think that all matters, even what may appear on its surface to be a humble bill such as this, will run into these difficulties until such time as we in this house are of sufficient stature to amend the constitution as
Interest Act
it so very badly needs amending today. I would point out to the hon. member that only recently a very beneficial Ontario statute, which purported to achieve the worthy ends that this bill attempts to achieve, was declared by the supreme court of Ontario to be unconstitutional. I refer to the Ontario unconscionable transactions act.
Under that legislation the province of Ontario had purported to legislate under their authority pursuant to section 92 of the British North America Act and their overriding authority with respect to property and civil rights. They had passed this bill which gave power to a county court judge to revise the interest rate or declare the entire transaction null and void if he should deem it to be unconscionable. This was a very meritorious piece of legislation which covered instances such as the hon. member may have in mind, where someone has been persuaded to sign a contract involving a very heavy interest rate without understanding what he is doing. The act was taken before the courts by some grasping and greedy finance company, no doubt, and ultimately the courts had to declare it unconstitutional and the very worthy purpose that this act had been serving for so many years can now no longer be achieved.
This is the kind of thing we should consider very seriously in this house. We should consider at the federal level whether the constitution could not or should not be amended, and again this is something that undoubtedly, according to precedent, would have to be done with the consent of the provinces, in order to provide either at the federal or provincial level clear, constitutional authority to legislate for the entire field of credit generally and certainly for consumer credit in particular. We know that banking comes under a federal measure and there again there is a conflict with regard to interest, banking, and private property and civil rights.
Here is an area where the joint committee of the house and the other place will be able to do something worth while, and surely in this area we can secure the co-operation of the provinces. While the Canadian constitution apparently has been beyond the ability of mere politicians to amend in recent years in any real comprehensive sense, at least in some areas we have made some headway in amending our constitution and I believe that in the area of consumer credit we would have a very good chance of obtaining the consent of the provinces, which is no doubt needed, to effect a new area of federal authority whereby consumer credit and credit in all its aspects could be controlled at the federal level. No doubt we could pass a statute analogous to the unconscionable transactions

Interest Act
act which would protect consumers of credit all over Canada in an equitable manner. I think if we amended the constitution to give the provinces individually entire authority in this regard the provinces might set up different standards throughout Canada with regard to the protection afforded to consumers of credit, and I do not believe this is something we want to do.
So I say I am in complete accord with the lofty and worthy objectives of the hon. member. I know that all members on this side of the house are willing to work very hard for a pervasive amendment of our constitution so that authority with regard to all fiscal and other legislative matters will be defined as clearly as possible within the constitution, thus leaving minimal areas where the new approach of co-operative federalism will hold sway. To as great a degree as possible, let us have a constitution that defines the rights and responsibilities of the various levels of government in such a way that they may be interpreted judicially as clearly as possible. We hope that the revising of the constitution can be carried out in the not too distant future, and when that is done I trust that the entire problem of consumer credit will find its proper place within comprehensive legislation which will protect consumers of credit all over Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISCLOSURE OF COST OF CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a few words I should like to say concerning Bill C-31 put forward by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nas-serden). I hope I shall abide by the rules and stick to the subject, as opposed to the hon. member who has just spoken.
No doubt is there much to be said in favour of Bill C-31, since it is designed to compel loan and credit companies to show on their contracts the interest rate to be paid by borrowers.
At first, that bill might seem attractive because, so far, there is no way for the borrower to find out exactly how much interest he will have to pay not only per year but per month.
However, following various pieces of legislation that were brought forward in the past and certain special taxes imposed by different governments, we realize easily after having studied the budget that the people get used very rapidly to formal changes, whereas there is really only one way to prevent certain abuses.
At the present time, finance companies are said to lend money at an annual rate of approximately 24 per cent and as there is no

indication on the contract, creditors may insist upon receiving amounts of money the borrower never thought he would have to pay.
The problem remains the same since, in many cases, people who apply to finance companies are known to be insolvent. They can then obtain credit by simply paying a much higher interest than the one charged by chartered banks and credit unions. I am pretty sure that even though finance companies were compelled to show in their contracts the amount of interest charged, that is 24, 26 or 20 per cent, this would in no way prevent people from applying for loans to those companies.
I feel that if the public is to be really protected, the answer is not to legislate on the methods to be used by finance companies, but to legislate mostly on the rate of interest charged by them, because, after all, the consumer is exploited when he has to repay large amounts of money.
Individuals whose credit is good enough may very easily obtain margins of credit from banks; evidently, those people are not involved.
The only persons involved are those who are denied any credit except by finance companies. This is why I respectfully submit that in spite of the interest which this legislation may arouse and in spite of the undeniable good faith of the hon. member for Rosthern, actually the public would not be sufficiently protected, unless finance companies are prevented by legislation from lending at prohibitive rates.
The hon. member for Rosthern mentioned that he had previously introduced a similar bill in former years and that its fate had been similar to that of all private bills. I think he could have put to good use the time his party was in office to enter this bill in the statutes.
In passing, I notice that section 2 of the bill states that the present act will come into force on September 1, 1962. I wonder how the hon. member for Rosthern decided to make his bill retroactive.
On the other hand, the member for Rosthern says that he wants to protect his constituents, when in fact he does not protect anyone because all those who will need money will know beforehand if they are going to pay 24, 26 or 20 per cent, whereas in the past they did not know. That will in no way prevent loans from being made, small consumers from being prosecuted before the courts eventually, or small consumers from losing by seizure of goods bought in good faith because of the bad faith of those who have loaned them the money.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I simply submit that this bill does not adequately protect the consumer and I would ask the hon. member to be kind enough to withdraw it.

maintopic: INTEREST ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISCLOSURE OF COST OF CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the sponsor of this bill. Contrary to what the previous speaker said, I maintain that even if the bill is not without fault and this I admit, it deals with part of the crucial problem which we are now facing. It is something, because in my opinion the sponsor of the bill has endeavoured to draw the attention of the house on the matter. Even if it had only enabled us to hear the statement made by the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene), I would say that this bill has provided the opportunity of hearing a lecture on constitutional principles.
One fact remains however and it is that today the people are swindled by a gang of illegal lenders and this nobody can deny. We are before an accomplished fact.
The federal government is being asked today to attempt to correct this unbearable situation and the hon. member for Renfrew South can only reply by putting a question. He even goes as far as to state that matter does not come under federal jurisdiction. For 90 years, it has been wondered whether it rests with the federal or the provincial governments to determine interest rates and the procedure to be followed for the granting of a loan. When the hon. member for Renfrew South maintains that the matter does not come under federal jurisdiction, he is absolutely not putting forward the views of his party. In my opinion, the present Liberal government has never had any scruples about taking over fields reserved to the provinces and even about infringing upon provincial rights.
I notice that neither the federal government nor the provinces feel responsible when the time comes to enact legislation to give some protection to the public and the small wage earner. However, when it is a question of protecting a company or a trust, everyone takes his responsibilities and looks after the company or trust concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the federal government has a role to play and that it must play it even to the point of seeking an agreement with the provinces, if necessary, to determine who is going to put a stop to this state of affairs which is leading the people down the road of bankruptcy.
The object of this bill is to make a credit financier criminally liable. In fact, the sponsor of the bill goes quite far, he even states his case boldly:
Interest Act
The purpose of this bill is to make a credit financier criminally liable when he does not, before the credit transaction, clearly disclose in writing to the debtor the cost of the credit calculated as a total dollar amount and as a yearly percentage of the credit amount to be granted.
That is the purpose of this bill. On the other hand, I feel that its ultimate end does not fulfil completely the aim sought today.
This criminal liability attaches only to the individual or company who grants the credit.
I would have liked the sponsor of the bill to indicate here some companies which do more than lend money at exorbitant rates and do not divulge them.
I consider charter banks as private companies which have the gall, with a deposit of $8 only, to loan $100 to the government. That is a crime.
I do not quite agree with the sponsor of the bill when he says:
The liability does not attach to the person who grants credit but not as a business-
As a matter of fact, I know personally several individuals who, today, loan money, without making a business of it, at even more usurious rates than the legally and officially constituted finance companies. That is why I said earlier that, in spite of that, there was some good in the bill.
Credit companies do not willingly give particulars of all interests included in sales contracts, and certainly the mover can attack interest rates, because that is where the evil is. Everything hinges upon that question. The companies use all possible means to try and hide the prohibitive amounts of interest which are added to the contract prices.
Here I should like to give you a few examples selected among the hundreds I know, because I myself have been in business, when I entered into numerous contracts and have been in some public offices.
I have here assertions by judges and lawyers to the effect that individuals lend at an interest rate as high as 75 per cent, and that it is impossible to take legal action against those thieves.
Nowadays, we go to great lengths to pass legislation in order to catch people who commit small larcenies, when for the last 90 years, we have not found ways to arrest those large scale thieves, to legislate with a view to preventing such thefts.
We must have legislation that will check what I would call "those big thieves". As we are discussing this matter today in the house, we can still hear hon. members declare that "it does not fall within our jurisdiction" or that "it does fall within the provincial jurisdiction". Who is to blame? We will have to assume our responsibilities tomorrow.

Interest Act
Let us take the following example. A man needs $5,000. Somebody comes to him and is willing to lend him the amount, provided that the borrower pays a 15 per cent commission, which amounts to $750. And one must add to this searching expenses, counsel fees, and so on. Formerly, such a transaction would have cost only $40, but nowadays- and I have seen contracts in a notary's office -a plain $3,000 insurance contract can cost $350. To the $750 commission you must add at least $300 in contract fees, which makes a total of $1,050 on a $5,000 loan.
Now, as it is not sure that the customer will make his first payment, an amount of $200 is withheld. That brings the cost of the loan to $1,250 so that the borrower will get only $3,750 out of a $5,000 loan.
Interest will be calculated on $5,000 for 36 months. At present rates, the interest will amount to $1,500 for 36 months and the borrower will have to make 36 monthly instalments of $200. If he always pays on time, he will reimburse $7,500 even though he has received only $3,750. That is one of the finest examples of such loans.
Here is another example. The same person borrows $5,000 on the same conditions from a private individual or from a private company this time, under what is called a small loans plan, a family plan or a budget plan. This is where things get out of hand. The borrower is told: "You will reimburse $7,500 in 36 months." However, the lender knows full well that the borrower will be in financial straits for two or three months, especially in marginal areas, and that it will be impossible for him to make his payments. The borrower who is a well-established and rich farmer, is told: "There is no hurry; take your time."
Three or four months later, when there is a downward trend on the markets, the borrower is reminded that he now owes $800. Then, the farmer who is pennyless and has nothing left says to himself: "It is useless; I will have to sell some stock or anything to pay that amount." But the lender reassures him once more: "No, do not hurry. We will just add the $800 to the $7,500 and you will repay the whole amount in 36 months."
And this keeps on until he realizes after three years that he has to repay $15,800 for a $5,000 loan. I have seen many such cases, Mr. Speaker.
It happens every day in our district, because-

This is right, they are thieves. I admit, Mr. Speaker, that we do not have any control on interests. The hon. member for Renfrew said so: "There is no limit on the interest rate". Nowadays, if an individual wishes to lend money at 300 per cent, you are unable to stop him. But if a labourer steals $3, you will have him jailed for a month, while the other individual will rob you blind and you will be unable to prosecute him.
There is another kind of case which I would like to bring to the attention of the house. I shall have to curtail my remarks, Mr. Speaker, because I do not want to kill this bill.
Mr. Speaker, I could mention several cases but, as my time is running out, I abbreviate my speech to enable another hon. member, who informed me of his wish to take the floor, to make a few remarks on the bill before us.
As a matter of fact, I myself introduced Bill C-23, which was more precise than this one, which wants to establish the interest rate. I have been advised to refer it to the committee on consumer credit. I readily did so. I was told that this would be the quicker way. Unfortunately, I find that the credit committee has, I think, become a rest room where nothing more is heard of the bill referred for consideration.

As this famous credit committee-I have been told so since, because at the time it had just been appointed, and I thought it quite adequate-seems to have been only set up to kill our bills in the gas chamber, it might as well not have been created at all.
We should, once for all, legislate to control this kind of business, because it has become quite shocking for this country not to be able to control or fix interest rates to stop usury. It should be our policy to fix interest rates, definitely and finally.
I shall now, incidentally ask the committee which is to study our bills, to accelerate matters a bit, give us a report and let us have the means of protecting each and every Canadian citizen against the loathsome business of those finance companies which are taking away our homes, our land, not only in my district but in the whole province of Quebec.
That is the problem in Quebec today. The federal government should act-if necessary, in agreement with the provinces-it should act once for all and give us some legislation to put the brake on such monstrous practice.

Mr. Speaker, in the limited time that I have available to me I wish to make certain comments on Bill No. C-31. Nine public bills on this subject have been referred to the special committee which this house set up on November 8 last. At that time the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught) moved a resolution to establish a select joint committee of the other place and of this house. It is interesting to note that the resolution states that a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons shall be appointed to inquire into and report upon the problem of consumer credit. It goes further and says this committee shall report upon the operation of Canadian legislation in relation thereto. The third section reads that the committee shall have power to call for witnesses, papers and records and examine witnesses.
Although all parties in this house were unanimous in the setting up of that committee, as they should be, and although the principle of this bill is the same as that of the other nine public bills, I think it would be quite improper if at this time we were to allow this particular bill to pass, although we are all in favour of its principle, when nine other public bills are before the select committee that has been set up. I am opposed to this type of amendment to the Interest Act at this time, because I am opposed to any piecemeal amendment to any legislation. We have had problems with the Income Tax Act and other legislation because it was amended piecemeal. We will also have problems with
Interest Act
this act if it is amended piecemeal. In my view, Mr. Speaker, the Interest Act should be completely reviewed and amended in total rather than sections thereof being amended piecemeal. I think the only way to deal with such an important piece of legislation is for the federal government to introduce a new act to deal with this particular problem.
The committee has the power to call before it persons, papers and witnesses. According to the information I have received, no other committee has ever been set up with this power to look into the problems of consumer credit. I think it is very important that before any legislation is introduced, as much as we may wish it to be implemented, such legislation should not be implemented without the committee calling witnesses before it who can deal with these problems. Not only should the committee call before it witnesses from the judiciary, from the bar associations across this country, from finance companies and people who deal in consumer credit and interest rates, but there should be a complete review of this matter right across the country. The committee should have before it evidence as to consumer credit, interest rates, collateral mortgages, chattel mortgages, conditional sales contracts, and so on. In this way we will receive recommendations from the select committee which can be incorporated into legislation that will deal with this problem.
The hon. member who introduced this bill stated that he first introduced it two years ago. I question his sincerity in introducing it again at this time, because he had two years in which to bring it forward and I gather from his remarks that he did not bring it forward last year. It seems strange to me that when his party was in office at that time, with a very large majority, such an amendment to the Interest Act was not implemented. I leave that with the house, Mr. Speaker, just as my own personal opinion.
As I stated, nine public bills have been introduced in connection with this matter. There was Bill No. C-10, an amendment to the Interest Act, which was referred to the committee; Bill No. C-55 was another proposed amendment to the Interest Act, which was referred to the committee; Bill No. C-14 was introduced, to amend the Small Loans Act, requiring statements of true interest rates. The bill before us at this time also includes this as one of its purposes. There was Bill No. C-23, an amendment to the Small Loans Act, to reduce maximum interest rates, which bill was also referred to the committee. Bill No. C-9 was another proposed amendment to the Small Loans Act, requiring statements of true interest rates, which was also referred to the committee. Then there was Bill No. C-33, a proposed amendment to

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys the Bills of Exchange Act, and Bill No. C-6, to provide control of consumer credit. To my mind there was a sound reason for the setting up of the select committee to deal with this matter, and we should not pass any piecemeal legislation to amend the Interest Act, the Small Loans Act or the Bankruptcy Act. The legislation which we all wish to see enacted is much too important to everyone to be treated in a piecemeal fashion.
Then there is the problem of education. It is very fine to have legislation, but legislation is only as good as it can be implemented and enforced. However, the problem here is that a man or woman who requires funds badly-and this is the reason for the high interest charges which people have to pay- go to finance companies and similar institutions to borrow money and do not care what rate of interest they have to pay, as long as they receive the money. After they have received the money and spent it, they complain about the high interest rates. That is why I say the problem here is also one of educating the people to be aware of the legislation which is enacted to improve this situation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in opening my remarks tonight I join with the minister in hoping that the estimates of his department, an extremely important one regardless of the

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
size of its expenditures, will pass this committee of supply tonight, in order to give him and his officials an opportunity to carry on with a most important phase of Canadian activity. I have said before in the house that I hope the minister will soon be in a position to give us and the Canadian people an indication of whether or not the provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act are to be carried on as they now stand, whether they are to be extended, or whether they are to be changed in some other way, in order that the mining communities throughout this country may have ample notice that changes are contemplated.
I know from previous conversations with the minister that he is anxious to bring before the house a statement as to the policy of the government after January 1 when, as hon. members may know, the provisions of the regulations under E.G.M.A., as we call it, run out. We fully realize that the purpose for which the special provisions under the act were introduced requires re-examination. When these measures were enacted into law, the emphasis was laid on gold production. In the years which have intervened, the provision of this special assistance which allowed mines in many areas to continue to operate, has been accompanied by social implications. We have found this out with regard to so many of the measures enacted since the second world war. For example, the closing down of a military base has tremendous social and economic implications, and such a decision must be weighed not only in terms of its direct effect but also in terms of its ancillary effects upon the Canadian economy, and in particular on the communities affected.
The provisions of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act were introduced by a Liberal government. They were continued in the period 1957-62 by a Conservative government, although I must say they were examined carefully and extended so as to recognize the new factors which were present. Perhaps for the first time, the provisions of this act were understood in the light of their social and human implications. This was a forward step. I intend to be brief, and my point is simply this: if changes are to be made, it is necessary that the minister be given an opportunity to announce them well in advance, so that the mining communities of Canada, and there are many of them, may know as quickly as possible what policy the government intends to follow in relation to this matter.
To come closer to the area in which I am more particularly interested, let me say that the future of the Northwest Territories is almost totally dependent upon mineral exploration and exploitation. For that matter,
the future of all Canada depends, in a way, on how well our mining companies are able to exploit the resources we possess. After all, two thirds of the pre-Cambrian shield lies in our northern regions. As the former prime minister so often impressed upon the Canadian people, ours is a northern destiny. It is to this area that Canada must look for much of its future welfare, and particular importance attaches to the possibility of exploiting the mineral resources which we know exist in the north, especially in the Northwest Territories. The reason I call attention to the emergency gold mining legislation is that for the years immediately ahead the exploitation of gold presents the greatest hope, because gold is a product which returns the greatest revenue per ounce when it is placed on the market.
In closing these brief remarks I wish the minister well in his efforts to make a statement of the kind I know he wishes to make, so as to reassure the mining communities all over Canada. I urge him to bring to his department any ideas which may be new or different. I have in mind the kind of suggestion which my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle made to his successor in office, namely that the role of a minister is to bring to his department a new approach. He should not simply accept the recommendations of his senior officials, though it is not my intention to disparage or detract from the dedicated and competent continuity which those officials bring to a department. I am merely suggesting that in the years which lie ahead, even though the hon. gentleman's department may now represent, relatively speaking, only a minor budgetary expenditure, it is likely to play an increasing role in the Canadian economy, as we take advantage of the fact that the door to the north has been opened in the past few years and that the north does have a potential greater than southern Canadians have ever dreamed.
At the same time, I urge the minister to bring to his department a large measure of flexibility in reaching the kind of decisions they will have to make. The areas we are opening up are different; we have different problems. This was recognized by the former government. I am sure the minister will carry on this policy of bringing in a fresh approach.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
First, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on his appointment to office. It may seem late to do so, but this is the first opportunity we have had. I do that on two grounds, the first of which is a purely personal one. If the minister thinks back to 1957 I believe he will recall he was the first member of parliament I met after I was elected in that year.

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys We met on the train going west. In the second place, I am also very pleased to see that a member from the north country, which is the real mining area of this great land of ours, a member who has lived all his life there and who understands us, is at present holding down this portfolio. I think it bodes well for the understanding required for this very important aspect of our economy.
In my remarks tonight I should like to deal in general with the gold mining industry. I think this is quite natural in that I represent a constituency that is almost completely dependent on that industry. I believe there is more gold produced in my constituency than in any other district in North America and, with the possible exception of one region of South Africa, than in any other place in the world.
We realize that the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act is going to have to be dealt with before the end of the year and it is not my intention tonight to deal with it at great length. We will have an opportunity later in the session to do so. However, the fact still remains that the act is so tied in with gold it is almost impossible to deal with the industry as a whole without touching on the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
I believe all hon. members have received a copy of the very excellent brief presented on behalf of the gold mining industry. It is entitled "Extension of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act" and is a submission to the federal government on behalf of the gold mining communities of Canada. I should like to deal with certain sections of the brief, as it tends to deal with the gold situation as a whole rather than particular aspects of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I will start on page 3 of the brief where it deals with the basic implications of the act that make the continuation of the industry possible. It has this to say:
Despite extensive mechanization which has helped restrain inflationary cost pressures-by reducing the number of employees-
My first objection to the brief is to that latter statement. I think that the industry does not have a proper or healthy outlook if they think that is the only way that inflationary pressures can be reduced. The brief continues:
-mining still requires considerable human effort. About 55 per cent to 60 per cent of mine operating costs go into wages and salaries. Mining is very much a "job creating" business.
This is very true, and as I develop my remarks further I should like to point out to the government how important this industry can be to the country and in meeting the problems that face our country at the

present time. For example, if you compare the job creating possibilities in gold mining with the job creating possibilities in the winter works program I think you can see the point I am trying to make. In the efforts of the present government to find some way to cure unemployment this is one place they could look with the hope of having very beneficial results. The brief continues:
For every $1 paid out in cost-aid a payroll of approximately $5 is protected, and a further expenditure of $2 made possible for operating supplies from many parts of Canada. This is a potent effect in human terms.
I should like to endorse that statement wholeheartedly. Any time that for the expenditure of $1 you can obtain the results outlined here is a very worth-while project indeed. The brief goes on to say:
The companies and people kept working, mainly as a result of the existence of the act, have paid back to the federal government probably close to 50 per cent (including sales tax) of the cost-aid received; and this percentage would, as we read the Quebec metal mining association brief, be close to 75 per cent if all levels of government were included. While it is true, of course, that these people get valuable services from their governments, too, it is also clear that cost-aid is by no means a complete loss for governments.
This again is a very good point to keep in mind. The present figures for emergency gold mining assistance do not necessarily represent a true picture of the actual cost to the government, because as a result of the money expended and pumped into the industry benefits accrue to the government so that the actual cost is far less, possibly 25 per cent or more less, than the actual assistance figures.
The fourth point made in the brief was a very important one.
No such accounting calculation can comprehend the far reaching secondary effects of the injection of federal funds. These effects multiply and echo through the national economy in diverse ways. The act therefore appears to us to be, in human terms, a productive expenditure program and not merely a package of more or less sterile transfer payments.
This, of course, is very true. The moneys paid for this purpose can turn up in many places. They can turn up in equipment and supplies needed to operate the mines and purchased from producers in other parts of the country. Some of these mines could only keep going because of assistance paid by the federal government in the past.
I should like to turn briefly to the gold situation throughout the world and more particularly the gold situation in the United States, because it affects us. If we refer to the brief again we find that at December 31, 1957 United States gold reserves stood at an alltime high of $22.9 billion while at that time only $11.9 billion was required to back United States currency. It is also pointed out that

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
despite the $15.2 billion in foreign short term dollar balances the dollar-gold position appeared to be reasonably good at that time.
The situation lias changed drastically since then. We find that by August, 1963 United States gold reserves had declined to $15.6 billion while the currency requirement had risen to $12.2 billion leaving a current margin of only $3.4 billion compared with $11 billion just six years ago. During the same time the value of foreign short term dollar holdings had risen $10.3 billion to $25.5 billion. The brief goes on to say that the United States faces a gold and foreign exchange crisis of unprecedented proportions for such a nation.
This points out, Mr. Chairman, the growing need for the production of more and more gold. As I have said, the brief is an excellent one. There are a few points I disagree with and possibly I can deal with them tonight. It is obvious, however, that a tremendous amount of work has been done on the preparation of the brief. I would urge all hon. members who have not read it to do so, because I think it will give them a much better picture of the gold situation than they have had previously.
The problems that have led up to this situation are listed on page 4. I quote from the brief:
World gold production has fallen far behind the growth rate required by expanding world trade under a gold exchange standard.
It may be said we are not on the gold standard, and that may be quite true. But the fact still remains that gold is the one commodity that is accepted anywhere in the world. It is one cash crop that any country would be glad to have. We in Canada are very fortunate in that we have gold reserves that have never even been scratched yet. The main problem is, how are we going to start developing them? If hon. members will look at the picture across Canada from coast to coast I think they will find that since the start of gold mining assistance in 1948 very few gold mines have gone into production. I know that there are none in my particular area of the Porcupine gold camp. No new producers have started since 1948. This is not because there is no more gold there. There is plenty of gold there. No one who has the wherewithal has been willing, under present circumstances, to put up the necessary funds to bring a gold mine into operation.
This leads us, Mr. Chairman, to look at the situation as it exists now. Over the last 15 years, since the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has been in effect, the Canadian taxpayers have poured some $170 million to $180 million into the gold industry. The situation today is not as good as it was back in 1948. It is true that a lot of good has
been done by this money. It has maintained a lot of mines, which in turn have maintained a lot of jobs, which in turn have maintained some gold mining communities. However, this measure is not the solution to the gold situation.
In the first place, I think we have to make up our minds just what we want to do in regard to gold production. We have to make up our minds if it is worth while to produce gold. I think anyone who has studied this problem will realize that gold is an almost indispensable product in the world today. Certainly, in so far as any country situated like Canada is concerned, it is extremely urgent that we do everything in our power to increase the gold production of this country. Let us face it, the day a gold mine opens it starts to die. Every day that goes by, every month and every year's production means that mine is that much closer to being finished. Regardless of whether or not we subsidize the mine to enable it to remain open, it is going to come to a close. Possibly if we had spent the money we have on the emergency gold mining assistance for the development of new mines, this country would be far better off than it is. Emergency gold mining assistance has not prevented Buffalo Ankerite from closing. It has not prevented the mines from closing and making Mata-chewan into a ghost town. It has not prevented Hollinger from announcing that it expects to close down at the end of next year.
We have to realize that the gold mines in the Porcupine camp are today about 50 years old and they cannot go on forever. Some two years ago the Hollinger gold mine poured a brick to celebrate $500 million of gold produced from that one property. It cannot go on forever. While we need this subsidy, as is explained in this brief presented to the government, to even maintain the status quo, what we really need in this country is a new mine to replace the Hollinger gold mine, and not a few more million dollars to extend the life of the mine for another year or two. We have ample evidence to show the need for the production of gold. I think we have ample evidence to show that we have the gold to produce. I think we have ample evidence to show that if the government takes the lead in ensuring the greater production of gold, it is going to solve many of the other problems with which we are faced, that is the serious ones. What we have to do is get on with this job.
As I mentioned earlier, it is not good enough to just pay this subsidy. This is not stimulating the gold industry. Unless we are prepared, as mentioned in the brief, to accept
4826	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys the fact the emergency gold mining assistance is an old age pension being paid to a dying industry, then it is time we took a new look at the gold mining industry. It is time that the government adopted a courageous and vigorous attitude in its attempts to solve these problems. I think we can go one step farther, Mr. Chairman. As I have said, the assistance the government has given in the past has not stimulated any new production. None of the mining companies seem prepared, seem to have the courage or the desire, to develop new gold mines.
I think this government should, first of all, show the industry that they really think that the production of gold is worth while and should be stimulated. The present gold mining assistance should be increased, but even more important I think the three-year time limit that has always been attached to it should be abolished. It takes about three years to develop a mine to the point where it starts producing. As long as a company is only sure of its future for a three-year period, it will not take that gamble. I feel that until a longer term is available, until you see fit to abolish the three-year time limit and extend it to a ten-year period or, better still, extend it until such time as a more realistic price is available for gold, new production will not be developed. The government should adopt this program so that the mining companies are prepared to keep this industry alive, because they know it is something the country needs. Furthermore, if the companies are not prepared to go ahead when they know the government is going to back them, then they should be told to step aside and allow the government to go ahead. I think this is something of vital importance to this country and it is something that should receive the full attention of the government.
