speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, although I am not an expert in mineralogy, I should like to make a few comments on the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
Like those who spoke before me, I should like to congratulate the minister for his report. In the course of his remarks, the minister blew his own horn because he had cut down the expenditures of the department by close to $2 million compared with last year.
At this stage, I wonder whether he deserves congratulations or blame. In order to reach a fair judgment, we must look into each item to ascertain which ones were cut down.
If he did cut down the expenditures of a probably top heavy administration of the

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of delaying in the least the adoption of these estimates, yet I am most anxious to make a comment or two on behalf of a desperately depressed mining area. But first of all may I congratulate the minister on his appointment and wish him well in his responsible position.
A few short years ago 2,500 men worked the Bell island mines in Newfoundland. Today only some 800 are precariously employed, never knowing from day to day just when their turn may come to receive the dreaded dismissal slip. And remember, Mr. Chairman, when a man is laid oft on this island it means much more than the loss of a job. It means his little home, so often the only tangible evidence of his years of employment, and often of frugality, is worthless, or nearly worthless. It means his whole life's investment in his community, school and
church is gone. The unemployed miner has to move away and no one wants his home. He can get little or nothing for what, in effect, is his whole life's savings.
I would urge the minister that he examine the possibilities of a subsidy. This would overcome the price handicap, if price handicap or price is a problem, and it usually is. I would also urge investigation into the possibility of establishing a direct iron or steel plant at the Bell island site, and I would once again urge the possibility or practicality of stockpiling.
A few days ago I was intensely interested to observe at first hand exciting experiments now being carried out by experts in the minister's department. We all anxiously await a technological breakthrough, but I know the department is moving steadily ahead, and in my opinion it is an enthusiastic and dedicated department.
Yet, with regard to Bell island, surely someone should be doing something positive about the Wabana situation. In my view there are two distinct aspects to the problem. The first is investigation of it. An assessment should be made of the precise minimum level of production at which the mine could continue to operate. This would require frank and open discussions with company management, by a board or by this department. The board should do a thorough analysis of the age, skill, sex, education, etc., of all those living on the island, and take an inventory of the island's social capital. Some of this information may be available, but it requires completion and analysis.
The investigational aspect would have to be backed up by a program of action approved and supported by the provincial and federal governments. It might be possible to bring some form of small economic endeavour to the island to support a part of the present population, particularly the older members of the community. In the main, however, the islanders require information as to the possible magnitude of the problem, possibly as to the federal assistance available for movement to jobs elsewhere, and as to retraining opportunities. To date, attempts to employ Bell islanders elsewhere in Canada have not been very successful. Some form of pension scheme for early retirement might be part of the answer. It has worked well elsewhere.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that Bell island could be symbolic. It could be symbolic of what this Canadian government can and will do for its own. I hope we can somehow arrange for Wabana to be an experiment in assistance-a kind of pilot plant, if you will; an example of the rekindling of human hopes and lives and the reconstruction of an economic area. Here we have, first of all, a
4828	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys concentration of population on a very small site, an island nine miles long, three miles wide, with a population of 12,000 to 14,000 Canadians. That very fact simplifies the initial problem of gathering the vital statistical information on which a plan of rehabilitation must be founded. It simplifies gathering the facts about education standards, aptitudes, interest in remaining on the island, and studying to acquire the academic knowledge essential to entering into a variety of technical and skilled occupations. On this kind of information an effective program can be founded that will attempt to deal in a well organized way with the many problems that are involved.
We have, apart from provincial resources with respect to education and vocational training, partial support during the completion of a training program, help in agriculture and fishing, among other things, and such organizations as the Atlantic development board, the new Department of Industry and other federal agencies. With all these powerful resources from which aid may be drawn, it should surely be possible to provide the solid basis for a viable community with a diversity of economic interests. It may not be expected that Bell island can show any measurable growth in population. The important thing at the moment is first of all to give those people hope. I repeat that this is a challenge to all the agencies, old and new, that exist in Canada for economic rehabilitation. Surely there are many, such as APEC, A.D.B., A.D.A., ARDA, plus a few provincial and federal ancillaries. The problem of Bell island cries out for solution, not sympathy.
A few evenings ago I noted with interest, some amusement and more amazement, a speech by the hon. member for Lapointe in which he discussed the possibility of tearing Newfoundland Labrador from Newfoundland. I think the same idea was expressed tonight by the hon. member for Roberval. They seem to have forgotten completely that Newfoundland Labrador was awarded to Newfoundland by the privy council in 1927 when Newfoundland was not Canadian, when I was not a Canadian. So that in effect Newfoundland, with confederation, brought Labrador back to Canada; not necessarily to Quebec, but certainly to Canada. This is one gift of the many that Newfoundland brought to Canada with confederation, and for which she has received very little credit.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have the opportunity this evening to pay my respects to a department which, during the time I was a minister of the crown, served me very well and won my complete admiration. Now as a member of the opposition I would like to


say in public in this house what I said in private to those in that department when I was a minister of resources. Knowing the workings of several departments, I do not think I am being unjust to any other department when I say with deep feeling that there is hardly a collection of officials in our government where so many brains, so much enthusiasm and dedication is concentrated in one area.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: How very nice of you to say that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I want to emphasize in my remarks this evening, as I welcome the new minister who is presenting his first estimates, that his department holds for Canada a very important place. They must always be, as they have been in the past, the eyes and ears of the development of Canada's resources. They are a department that has gone ahead and surveyed our country, mapped it and put the research into a form that private business and other governments can use. We see large newspaper headlines when a private company discovers some mineral or oil resource, but usually the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, in some report sometimes hidden away in their files for many years, has already indicated the possibilities of such a find in that area. This applies to such dramatic finds as those in Blind River, as well as the oil surveys and showings in the northern territories.
Therefore this department is providing tremendous assistance to private enterprise in providing maps and information for use in exploration. Those who are going out to locate minerals or petroleum products underneath the surface of our soil would be wise always to send their exploration people first to the files of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. If they search those files carefully they will usually get the clues as to where to look, and thereby save a great deal of time and money.
My remarks this evening on the various programs of the department will be, I hope, exceedingly brief. I would like to say that I hope the new minister adds his weight to that of previous holders of this office in supporting the extended hydrographic program. The announcement made by the minister in the house recently indicates that this will be done. I also hope the minister will continue to support previous ministers in regard to the oceanographic institute in Halifax. The report given by the minister recently indicates that this will be his attitude.
One may wonder as to the importance of a hydrographic survey and an oceanographic

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
institute. I recall that I once asked, when I first became minister, how long it would take to find out the depth of the sea off our shores at the rate at which we were proceeding at the time we assumed office. The answer was-I suppose it was an estimate-that at the rate we were proceeding in 1957, it would take 250 years. So we embarked upon a program of doubling the hydrographic service areas and we cut that figure down to half. What I am really saying is that this increase in program, such as the new program of shipbuilding, and so on, that is being put into operation, means we can concentrate on where the need is, and instead of our having to go to the United States navy and have them carry out a hydrographic survey for us to find out how deep are the waters off our shores, or what is the access for other countries, we will have the facilities in our own department. I am glad the minister has shown an understanding of the importance of this program in the long range planning of the development of our resources.
There was one program about which 1 wanted to speak with some feeling this evening, but I have decided not to go into it too deeply at this time. I refer to the polar continental shelf program. I hope the minister is watching this program very carefully. I think he understands and fully appreciates the tremendously important results of the work now being undertaken under this program.
It will be recalled that in 1958, at the law of the sea conference in Geneva, four articles were passed by the conference. One of them said that land under the sea off the shores of any country was the property of that country as far out as it could be developed. As far as I can find out from the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, this acquisition of the right to explore and develop the continental shelf off our shores has added approximately one eighth to the area of Canada, roughly 12 to 13 per cent. If we had gone out and by force of arms added one eighth to our resource area, this would have been a great headline story in all the papers around the world. But because the nations of the world in free discussion made this part of international law, we have added to our territories this immensely valuable resource area. Indeed, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys started immediately on a polar continental shelf program to explore this very valuable additional territory.
At this moment I should like to suggest to the minister that the polar continental shelf is a co-ordinated program, with all types of scientists engaged in a study of that area. It was no accident that we started on the
northern fringes of the islands. It is no accident that we are working back into the Arctic archipelago in order to get the information we need. But I now suggest something about which there is no urgency but which should not be forgotten. We cannot find out all about the geology of our continental shelf and of our islands in the Arctic archipelago or the north generally until we know more about the earth's surface below the Arctic ocean.
I would remind the minister that a conference was called in Calgary under the auspices of the Canadian geological association some three years ago in which the nations of the northern hemisphere brought all their knowledge to bear and had a series of discussions about Arctic geology. This conference was very valuable to all the nations which attended. Many of us were tremendously impressed and awed at what seemed like the tremendous knowledge of the Arctic ocean of the neighbours of Canada across the Arctic ocean, namely the U.S.S.R. Some of us hoped at that time that this example of a conference of the northern nations concerning Arctic geology would be carried forward into an active program participated in by many of the countries of the northern hemisphere in a systematic attack on finding out what we need to know about the earth's surface underneath the Arctic ocean, so as to know more about the geological province which lies adjacent to our country.
We are completing at the present time a tremendous world-wide program known as the geophysical year. I think the actual physical work has been completed for some two or three years, but the accumulation of all the papers is still going on. Here is an example of the countries of the world co-operating, moving into each other's territory and finding out about the earth's surface in a massive, world-wide co-operative effort, in this program we know as the geophysical year. Would it not be a good suggestion if we could apply this co-operative approach to having the nations of the northern hemisphere start thinking in terms of a joint program supported by all these nations on finding out about the geological province which exists underneath the Arctic ocean? It would be of great value not only to the United States because of its interest in the state of Alaska, but also to Canada with a great area in the north. This would apply as well to the Danes, the British, the Norwegians, the Swedes, the Finns and the Russians. I think all these nations would gain tremendously from such a joint program. I know we are not very far advanced with the subject of oceanography; other countries are away ahead of us. We need to know more about these currents, so as to know how to use them to our advantage.
4830	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
But on the question of the earth's surface, about which I was speaking, I hope the suggestion I have made will be considered by the minister over the next two or three years and that this idea will not be dropped. The original credit for it goes to the geological association of Canada, but I hope the government will always be in a willing mood to discuss this with any country. As hon. members know, the previous government offered to the Russians co-operation in making available that information which we had, if they did the same for us. I hope that this same offer will be continued by the present government.
I should like to conclude my remarks, Mr. Chairman, with a short statement on the ground water surveys in western Canada. In that area, like many other parts of the country, we are face to face at all times with the necessity of obtaining water supplies. We have made a move or two to reserve some of the surface water in the prairie areas through our dug-out programs, our dams on the streams running into the stems of the major rivers, our dams on the Saskatchewan river and the Qu'Appelle river, the irrigation works in Alberta, and I hope also one of these days the dams which will be constructed in the eastern Rockies. We are doing a fairly good job with the surface water, but of course other things of tremendous moment have to be done in the next ten or 20 years. However, I hope that the ground water component of the water supplies to the western prairies are not overlooked.
I know that in the final analysis the discovery of water in underground sources, whether it be in a river or in a great underground pool, and whether it is salty or potable, will depend on the drilling of wells; and this is exorbitantly expensive. But knowing the tremendous genius of the scientists of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, I think that a technique can be evolved that at least gives some indication where to look when we have to start a well drilling program. I hope that what we put into the estimates some time ago will enable a start to be made on a groundwater survey program by air to see if this technique could prove out and be proceeded with, because the actual first work which was started was very tentative. I hope the program commences at the United States boundary in Saskatchewan and works its way north, because there is a desperate need for some sort of water supply greater than we can get on the surface. If the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys can point the way towards these underground rivers and these underground pools of water, if they are in sufficient quantity I can assure the house that the


monetary return to the general wealth of Canada will be immediate, because several chemical operations would start up all through that portion of the so-called Palliser triangle if water supplies were available for chemical operations.
If we want to provide diversification of industry in Canada and if we want to strengthen those areas which are too dependant on a one-product economy, then this particular area of southern Saskatchewan is one sector of the country where we would like to see the ground water table survey extended and continued. I know that the item of cost is not very high because I am not asking that there be a well drilling program, although this will have to come eventually. But I should like to see whether the genius which I know exists in the department could not be brought to bear on the airborne technique, which would give us indications of where water supplies are underneath the surface of the earth.
That is all I intend to say for the moment, Mr. Chairman, but I do want to serve notice on the minister that I will be asking some questions on these matters I have raised in more detail when we reach items 40, 70, 75, 80, 90 and 130.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I too should like to say a few brief words about the mining industry and the estimates of this department. However, before doing so I should like to congratulate the minister on his appointment. Coming as he does from a mining area, he is bringing considerable knowledge and competence to his department. Personally I have heard nothing but good of him as well as of his officials in the operation of his department since his appointment. The main burden of my remarks will be the mining industry in relation to the rest of the country, and its growth, and more particularly the operation of the mines department in the context of all the government's activities. These certainly need to be co-ordinated if we are to obtain the best of all possible worlds.
The mining industry has grown very rapidly. It has grown more rapidly than our other principal resource industries. This is a fortunate thing for Canada because considerably more than half of this great nation of ours can produce only mineral resources as a major product. Agriculture is limited in extent. Even our forests are limited in area. But our territories which can produce minerals are vast indeed and encompass not only the land area of the nation but the continental shelves, and many of the lake and river bottoms. So it is fortunate that the mining industry is expanding and that the future holds

promise of an even greater expansion than most of the primary activities of this country.
It is a big volume industry which depends very much on international trade. If it is to produce more jobs for Canadians it must contain a great deal more processing within its compass. This is where a good many jobs in the future lie. The mining industry has become immensely more efficient, so employment in the mines themselves is not a major source of income in this country. It has to be in respect to producing the machinery, the capital goods required, the transportation systems and, more especially, the processing plants that employment must be sought. Here is where the great prospects for employment and income lie.
The industry has to look much further ahead than in years gone by. The big investments necessary are made only in the light of long term market analyses. This is another reason why the government is well advised to be making its plans, not on an annual, but on a five-year basis. Contracts should be awarded for more than one year at a time. In this way the mining industry will obtain more guidance from the government and be able to make sounder investments. The market analyses carried out by the government economists, the mineral specialists in the resources division and those who work with them should be looking over the entire field to see what is happening, not just with regard to minerals but with regard to competitive materials. In the field of energy, for example, we should not focus our attention upon only one means of production, be it oil or coal or nuclear power. We should be looking across the entire field to weigh up the competition and how the market should be shared. This is one of the reasons why activities in government should be co-ordinated to a greater extent.
In the field of energy we have the national energy board concerned primarily with oil and natural gas. The Department of Trade and Commerce is concerned with the export of various by-products. The department of northern affairs is concerned with waterpower, the new Department of Industry with atomic energy and the mines branch with the coal. It is all very well if these activities go on separately with respect to the purely technical side of their administration. It might be satisfactory to have these things compartmentalized, but there has to be a measure of co-ordination especially where market analysis is involved. Perhaps this could be done in a summary way under the new national economic council, but I suggest that it would be better if more of these activities were transferred to the national energy board. I am thinking now in particular about market studies and trade prospects, the guide lines
Supply

Mines and Technical Surveys we shall be using to determine which areas of investment are most attractive, which warrant more government assistance, and so on; in other words, the orientation of these programs in the general context of business prospects is essential.
I should like to boost the mineral resources branch which certainly has been looking at longer term prospects of this industry. It is beginning to look abroad and I trust its activities are being co-ordinated with those of the Department of Trade and Commerce with respect to world markets, trading arrangements and so on.
The surveys and mapping branch has been in existence for a longer period of time. Its extensive reports over the years have been a virtual mine of information to prospectors who have spent their winters reading in well thumbed notebooks where the occurrence of one mineral or another has been recorded. From such information as this have come important discoveries. From the more extensive surveys has come the elaborate data necessary for the discovery of big volume resources such as oil, industrial minerals, potash, salt and so on. Then there are the aerial surveys promoted by this department. These have provided a great source of information for Canadian industry. Aerial surveys, magnetic surveys and the like can be carried on under contract in other countries. The Colombo plan has provided an outlet for this type of expertise, and a new Canadian industry of this character has grown up largely as a result of the activities of this branch of the department.
The mines branch has done a tremendous job with regard to the processing of minerals, chemical extraction techniques and so on. The new nickel extraction industry on the prairies is one of the products of this research program. The upgrading of iron ore is also carried on. New mineral resources have been developed and their processing has been advanced. The processing of uranium has largely been perfected by the mines branch in Ottawa. Many new developments are likely to take place in the future and I can think of one in British Columbia which is typical of the prospects which are now before us. These will result from increased investment in research and processing techniques. I refer to extensive coal deposits on the edge of my own riding, one of the largest in western Canada. This is undoubtedly one of the cheapest sources of energy on this continent, if not in the whole world. It contains a high percentage of ash. This ash is rich in alumina, the raw material from which aluminum is produced. Today we import this product from foreign countries; yet here, in a large coal
4832	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys deposit in western Canada, is a vast supply of this raw material. The mines branch can carry out research on raw materials such as these and help develop techniques which are best suited to the resources of this country so as to make us increasingly self-sufficient with respect to raw materials.
I have been stressing the importance of research. Research, generally speaking, must itself be referred to as a growth industry. Certainly, it is one of the fastest growing industries on this continent; it has been roughly doubling in size every five or six years. No other industry can match this pace. It is an industry of ideas, and one idea tends to give birth to another. As I say, this expansion is going on and we should not leave too much initiative to other countries. We should concentrate this generation of ideas upon the areas of greatest advantage to our resource industries and, more particularly, upon the processing of our raw materials. The mines branch is doing just that. This is one of the reasons why I personally would urge that proportionately, and in the aggregate, considerably more money should be spent in mineral research, processing research and research in the area of mining in this country. Such research will result undoubtedly in unique resources attracting unique processing industries, and we will attract and hold industries which will last and will be more competitive than some of our secondary industries in international trade. Because they are essentially unique they will be located in the more remote outlying areas of Canada, which are otherwise very difficult to develop.
I have really been emphasizing in my remarks the fundamental economics of not only much of Canada, but all of Canada. To a large extent we are living off our resources. Mining, like forestry and agriculture, is one of our great bread and butter industries. This industry deserves considerable attention and support. Personally I do not believe in subsidies. I believe that the government can help through research, through negotiations in respect of tariff barriers and encouragement of further processing. However, subsidies may occasionally be necessary and if they are necessary they should be introduced with the idea of eventually tapering them off and eliminating them in the long run. This requires at the same time long term forecasting, looking well ahead, long term research, research aimed at the second and third decade.
I believe that in the mines branch this sort of thing is going on. In my view, more of it should be carried on in Canada, and I believe we are well on our way to improving our


economic lot and finding jobs for Canadians in parts of Canada which otherwise would not develop as rapidly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would feel I had not discharged my duty tonight if 1 did not make a few remarks on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. First of all, I wish to associate myself with other members in expressing congratulations to the new minister on his presentation of the estimates for the first time. I have known the genial minister for a number of years. I have also had a close association with the officials of his department and I have found them to be intelligent and sympathetic in helping to solve some of the problems in my riding. They are greatly appreciated indeed.
I should also like to associate myself with the remarks made a few minutes ago by my colleague, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, when he referred to the fact that we should not treat the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys as an insignificant department. When I think of the policy of the former government in developing roads to resources and the surveys that have been made by members of this department together with members of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and realize the great potential for the future that lies not only in those parts of Canada with which we are more familiar but in some of the areas of the north that have been mentioned, my only regret is that I will not be around 50 or 100 years from now to see what actually develops in this regard. Looking into the future I see a terrific amount of work and a terrific development in the department, and the contribution it will make to the standard of living in Canada in particular, and in the world in general.
As I come from an agricultural area in Saskatchewan where 60 per cent of Canadian wheat is produced, some members may wonder why I am taking the time of the house to discuss matters having to do with mines and technical surveys. I believe I mentioned on another occasion in the house, and I repeat it now, that 20 per cent of the coal deposits in Canada lie within the boundaries of my riding of Moose Mountain. Twenty per cent of the lignite coal deposits in Canada are centred around Bienfait and Estevan. These deposits, together with our agricultural resources, make up a large part of the industries and resources of my riding, and as the member for that riding I wish to bring certain matters to the attention of the house and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
In passing may I say I appreciate very much the attention that the coal industry has

been given in my riding. I recall now the fact that recently Mr. Mel Brodie was appointed to fill the recent vacancy on the dominion coal board. Years ago Mr. Brodie's father pioneered the development of the coal industry in that part of Saskatchewan and this work is now being carried on by his illustrious son. This appointment has stimulated a great deal of interest among coal producers in that area.
Another move that was greatly appreciated and which was undertaken by the former government under the Leader of the Opposition and the former minister of mines and technical surveys was the amendment of the Coal Production Assistance Act. Under the old act passed by the house in 1949 we found ourselves greatly handicapped in that under that act approximately 30 cents a ton at the pithead was required to repay a loan. This sounded fairly reasonable, but it was more or less based on the fact that the wholesale cost of hard or anthracite coal was around $9 to $10 a ton at the pithead, and 30 cents a ton for the repayment of loans was not too big an obstacle to overcome. However, when this formula was applied to lignite coal, which is worth about $1.90 to $2 a ton at the pithead, 30 cents a ton percentagewise was exorbitant and worked quite a hardship on coal production in our area. Since the application of the new amendment to the Coal Production Assistance Act the repayment factor has been cut down from 30 cents to 18 cents a ton, and this has greatly assisted and accelerated coal production in our area and has made the prospects of economic stability for the industry a lot brighter.
There is another thing I should like to mention in passing, which was referred to in the house a month or two ago by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he made a statement on the attitude of the government so far as the national energy board is concerned. He referred to the fact that the present government was going to follow through on the policy espoused by the former government with regard to the development of a national grid system in Canada. We know that sources of power are the sinews of industry. A few moments ago I referred to the fact that in the riding of Moose Mountain we have 20 per cent of the total lignite coal deposits in Canada. Naturally the people of that area are very interested in the development of a national grid system because here in the centre of Canada there is a great source of cheap power that could be fed into such a system and, of course, directly and indirectly this would enhance the economy of that whole area.
At the present time the Saskatchewan government has quite a large steam-turbo power
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys generation development at Estevan, Saskatchewan in which I believe there has been an investment of about $40 million, but this development is only in its infancy compared with the total potential. I believe the production cost now is somewhere in the neighbourhood of three to four mills per kilowatt. Engineers understand more about the production of power than I do and they will appreciate the fact that this is a very low cost factor and that the possibilities are terrific if we think of the development of power in the future in the area in and around Estevan, and the feeding of this cheap power into a national grid system. As I say, we are looking forward with great anticipation to the enhancement of our economy by this development in the years to come.
I think the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys will also be interested in becoming more acquainted with the fact that along with coal production in our area there is a vast oil production development in Saskatchewan, particularly in the southeastern part of the province. The figures I have available to me indicate that something like 5,025 or 5,028 producing wells are now active in the province of Saskatchewan and I was very happy to find on checking further that over three quarters of them are in southeastern Saskatchewan within the boundaries of my riding.
This, in itself, in the opinion of a lot of people, is going to enhance the economy of that part of the province. Of course, anything that can be done under the national energy board to further expand the market for oil is naturally going to be of great interest to the people in Saskatchewan. We want to fully develop not only our agricultural resources, but we want to become known for the industrial and mineral development in our province. We want to develop a reputation that we do not live by bread alone.
There is another development in our corner of the province about which I want to question the minister later under some other item in his department. I refer to the production of clay products. We make some of the finest bricks in western Canada at Estevan, Saskatchewan. They are made by Saskatchewan Clay Products. For some reason that I have not been able to discover, we have not found a large market for these bricks. They have not been used in the construction of federal buildings. I have had a number of inquiries on this point, and I am going to make a further investigation in order to ascertain whether this is due to some weakness in our purchasing system or to some flaw in the product itself. If there is some flaw in the product, we would like to know about it. We have not, as yet, had a

Mines and Technical Surveys definite answer as to why Estevan clay products have not been used in the construction of federal buildings.
We have, of course, other minerals in Saskatchewan apart from those found in my area. I do not want to usurp the time of the committee, but I think most members are aware of the fact that Saskatchewan has become the leading potash producer in the world. In the riding of Melville, a short distance north of Moose Mountain, we have the International Chemical Company potash development. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with others who have congratulated the minister on his appointment to this office. I do so for two reasons that have not been mentioned. The first is a very important one, and that is the fact that the minister comes from northern Ontario. Second, he is the only member of the cabinet with the political affiliation of Labour-Liberal. I think both of these facts are to his credit.
The department of mines, Mr. Chairman, has been of great importance to a large segment of our economy. I think it is of interest to look at the department of mines in conjunction with a number of other departments, because these departments have problems which are similar in nature. I refer to the departments of mines, forestry, fisheries and industry. The Department of Agriculture, as everyone knows, has received more attention from the members of parliament than probably all the other resource departments put together, because of the rural representation we have had in parliament for years.
However, there is a division of responsibility between the province and the federal government in each of these resource departments. I am sure that the people interested in these resource industries find their connections with the provincial departments much closer than with the federal departments. I am not one of those who think that this is a good thing. I believe it may be to

the advantage of many of those engaged in these industries if there were an extension of the jurisdiction from the federal field into the provincial field, rather than a division. I think this is true of the department of mines, just as it is true of several others.
We in northern Ontario look to the department of mines as an indication of what is going to happen in connection with the newly formed Department of Industry. We have found that very little more was accomplished as a result of the establishment of the Department of Forestry than had been accomplished in the past. In spite of the raves that preceded the introduction of that department, the results have not been spectacular in so far as individuals engaged in that field have been concerned. This, of course, has been true of the department of mines as well. There are very few miners, I would suggest, in this country who have ever met a representative from the federal department of mines. This does not mean that the federal department of mines has not been very active in their affairs or interested in their problems. However, the contact between the federal department and the miner, or those working in the mines, has been slight to my knowledge.
The same situation prevails, of course, in other departments. The reason I put forward these suggestions is that we are looking back at mining to some extent in my part of the country and looking forward to the Department of Industry being able to accomplish some of the things that have not been accomplished by the development of primary industries. Timiskaming, in common with other like areas, is looking forward and hoping that some of the problems that have developed in the past will not be carried forward. This is my reason for comparing the two departments.
We have in Timiskaming, in common with the hon. member for Timmins, a major portion of the gold mine production of Canada. As the years go by this production continues to decrease. It is true that in my riding we have a new producer on the horizon. It is true also that since the report of the emergency gold mining assistance was presented, two mines that were in production then have ceased production. It is to be expected, of course, that there will be a continuation of prospecting and developing of gold mines, but this is something that is not going to be discussed during the consideration of these estimates because it involves the Department of Finance as well. However, the storm warnings are flying across the world indicating the need for a discussion of the relative positions of gold and silver

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
in the monetary affairs of the world. At the moment there is a shortage of these two basic commodities, gold and silver.
The United States is being pressed to make concessions in connection with both of these commodities and has already done so to a limited extent in connection with silver. Very little has been done about the problem of world demand, Mr. Chairman, but some of these problems could be solved if the price of gold were set at $100 per ounce. There are those who would say this is unrealistic, and I am not the one to say whether it is or is not.
The government has received many representations on this subject. Only recently the Prime Minister was given a copy of a presentation from a Mr. Crump who has been making suggestions on international monetary matters for some time. He presented his latest one to the Prime Minister on May 29 last, and pointed out that the problem in relation to gold in the international field is as serious today as it was in the 1930's. He pointed out that in the United States in the 1930's $60 billion in currency and deposits was backed by only $4 billion in gold. Then, because the problem became acute, the United States raised the price of gold from $20.67 an ounce to $35 an ounce, but the situation has not got any better. It has gone from bad to worse, because the amount of currency is increasing by $300 million annually and is only backed by $16 billion in gold.
I am not going into an argument as to whether we should have the backing of gold for our basic transactions, but Canada should study this matter and see what it can do to its own advantage. If the price of gold goes up, there are very few countries in the world which would benefit to the extent Canada will. We have large exports of gold at present, and in my opinion if the price of the product could be raised substantially we would increase the value of our exports.
However, we have been told, "Let's not rock the boat." I remember the former minister of finance replying to a question of mine, which asked whether the government intended to press for an increase in the price of gold at an international monetary fund meeting, and he said, "Good heavens no; we will rock the boat; something may happen." I have thought about that answer a great deal in the interim. I have also read a lot on the subject and I am of the opinion that the only way it could rock the boat would be to our advantage.
But if this were not the case, then so what? If the price dropped completely out of the market, so what? Unless it is given another shot in the arm the gold mining industry is already on the downhill slope. In my riding 28902-5-308
the largest producer of gold on the North American continent faces a very limited life because of the depletion of ores and because of the geographical situation. Therefore unless Canada is interested in facing the problem of gold and what to do with gold in relation to its economy, the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, and other crutches we supply will not be of much advantage.
I know we will be discussing E.G.M.A. later this year, and we will be asked to extend this legislation. I do not expect there will be another 25 per cent boost in the payments, such as was provided last year. I have not heard any rumours which would lead me to believe this is going to happen, but I think the minister should indicate that he will remove the word "emergency" from the title of this act, because this would stop municipalities and gold mining communities having to come to Ottawa time after time asking for a continuation of this emergency aid.
The act was passed in 1948 as a remedy. It did not provide the full remedy, but it is a crutch upon which the industry has been hobbling along, and that crutch will have to remain until the industry ceases to produce gold. Let us be realistic and decide what amount gold should cost on the international market, and how we can actively press for that price.
In addition to representing the gold industry and one of the largest iron mines in the nation, I also represent nine of the 11 primary silver producers in Canada. This industry is being treated in much the same way as the gold mining industry, except that for years the gold mining industry has been able, through highly priced, successful lobbyists, to bring its grievances to the attention of the government in a much better way than the silver industry.
There is a world shortage of silver, and the industry should be given government assistance for stockpiling purposes. It is located in a sufficiently small area and is controllable enough for the federal government to be able to buy its total production for coinage, if for no other use. We all know silver has two uses, one a monetary one and the other industrial. It is a very valuable substance, but the decline in the supply of silver is causing the United States government grave concern.
Its price has been raised from 91 cents to $1.29 to protect the supply which the United States has, but not enough is being produced and used for industrial purposes. Here again the federal government should do more to assist the silver industry. If it did we would not have the Minister of Finance getting up, as he did the other day, and saying not enough silver dollars could be minted for those who wished to buy them.

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
If the price of silver were to reach its own level, without the restraints that have been placed on it by the United States, the price would rise rapidly and many of the industry's problems would be solved. I believe the federal government should get more control and involve itself deeper in the production of silver, particularly from the refinery stage onwards. The previous government signed a contract with the Cobalt refinery whereby it agreed to purchase a sizeable sum of silver from this refinery, but until all the mines in the area take part in supplying the refinery, difficulty will arise in maintaining a price which will be competitive with the smelter in Montana. So long as the federal government co-operates, as it has done in recent years, in making concessions in the freight rates on ore being shipped to the United States, it will be difficult to encourage the Canadian mines to ship their silver locally.
One of the big producers finds that until this refinery is in a position to give a guarantee of being able to handle all their silver at a set, agreed rate and provide guarantees that will make it possible for them to reach this long term agreement, they are not in a position to give up their contracts in the United States.
I think some sympathy has to be given to the company, because they were dealing previously with a Canadian company, and when the Canadian company decided to fold up, this left the Canadian producers without markets and they had to go outside our country for the refining of their product. This meant, of course, that the Canadian government had to go to the United States to buy back the silver that we use for coinage purposes. I think that we as a growing nation, a nation not only of one nationhood but several, should be in a position to supply our own coinage from silver that is refined in this country and delivered to the mill. I suggest this program should be undertaken. It is not very much to ask for, because I am told that our silver meets the requirements of the Canadian mint and I think the industry has been able to convince the provincial and federal governments that there is a need for establishing the guarantees necessary to allow the mining industry to deal with this refining.
The silver industry would like other things. It would like the assistance of the department in bringing to the attention of the minister's colleague in the Department of Finance the need for providing silver producers with the same precious metal mines depletion allowances that have been provided for gold producers. All mines, of course, receive a depletion allowance, and the gold mines are in a more favourable position than silver


producers. We think the precious metals depletion allowance should be applied equally to silver producers. I ask for the intervention of the minister in this connection because until the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys considers silver to be a precious metal under the terms of the act, it is doubtful whether the Minister of Finance will consider the tax exemptions that would accrue from this designation.
We in northern Ontario desperately need a geological survey conducted by the federal government. We believe this would be worth the government spending a considerable sum of money in accomplishing. Hon. members will remember the history of Canada back in the days of the silver boom of 1904 in Cobalt. Certainly I do not have to tell hon. members of this house the history of the gold mining industry in northern Ontario. I am quite sure every member here has a relative who either became very rich or went bankrupt because of buying stocks in some of the mines in the early days of Cobalt. I am sure there are in parts of Canada other than in northern Ontario rooms in houses which are papered with mining stock that is about as valuable as wallpaper today, except for its souvenir value. This was an area of fabulous wealth. The survey carried out by the federal government so long ago is now greatly out of date and could be added to immensely by a survey conducted by the government at this time.
We are on the edge of the pre-Cambrian shield, an area of proven mineral wealth, and it seems to me that until the day governments -and this day does not seem to be getting any closer-are able to meet the problems mentioned by the hon. member in regard to Bell island, by the hon. member from Cape Breton island, by the hon. member from Timmins, and the hon. member from Alberta in regard to strip coal, we are not going to solve the problems that must be solved in these areas. Each of these areas was built around a primary producer and many of these problems have arisen because the areas have been unable to make the transition to industry. We have this department and its facilities, and I ask the minister to give consideration to carrying out a geological survey in depth, as the thinkers of the nation now say. We do not mind how they do it, whether by diamond drilling or otherwise, but the survey should be of a type similar to that carried out in United States. In that country anyone can go into the library and find out the potential of a particular area. They can ascertain whether there is a potential in an area by research at the library. It would seem to me that many of the prospectors who are now covering areas that have been well covered

so many times before would find it advantageous to know what possibilities may exist in areas that they have not considered to be lucrative in days gone by.
I know the department has expanded. I was going to refer to the committee report of a few years ago, which said-and I thought they were being very foolish-that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys should go out and buy new buildings, hire more people, and so on; in other words, they should expand. I always think it is foolish to tell senior civil servants to do this, because they seem to do it by themselves. However, I know this department has expanded. We were told this evening by the former minister of northern affairs and national resources that people have been added to the department, and I am quite sure this is so. The department has been highly complimented by many of the mining companies in my area on the work they have done in the fields of dressing, preparation and new methods of handling ores. The most recent of these accolades came from the Jones & Loghern Company in the United States which is developing the Adams iron mine at Dane. This company is well equipped to handle a great deal of their own development and refining processes, and yet they have nothing but praise for the officials in Ottawa who have helped them, when requested, in the dressing field.
I would also like to urge the minister to give consideration to the many new techniques being used in mining, and the difficulty of obtaining designations that would indicate the change in the type of mining. I am referring in part to the developments that have taken place in this field, where instead of drilling a shaft and doing the mining in this way, they are now drilling holes and using hydraulic processes to extract minerals. I think this is an ideal method of mining. I hope to see the day in Canada when many of the coal fields that we have will be operated by drilling, burning and distilling, thus obtaining the benefits of the mining resource in this manner.
I think it is unfortunate that the act is so difficult, or appears to be so difficult, to change in order to bring up to date the wording to allow for changes in the new types of mining which develop at any time. I hope that during the forthcoming year the minister will give consideration to this major problem that we have in monetary metals, the gold and silver ores, to see whether we can devise some system that will allow the mining industry certain-you might call it free enterprise-* opportunities, so that if gold will sell at a price that is profitable to the mining communities, and the mining companies quite often think this is possible, they will have 28902-5-308J
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys this opportunity. I do not think it means throwing them out on the free market, but we could help to develop in the international monetary field the role that Canada must play as an exporter of silver and gold metals.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to join the other speakers in congratulating the minister upon his appointment. I know that experience, ability and affability are enjoined in him in such happy proportions that it portends well for the future of his department.
I rise to tell hon. members of the committee a brief story which, while local in origin, coming from the riding of south Renfrew, I think has a moral which may be of interest to all hon. gentlemen in general and to the minister in particular. I rise to tell the story of Calabogie. Calabogie is in the township of Bagot and Blythfield in my riding and is situated on the banks of the roaring and majestic Madawaska river. The Calabogie area was developed when Bytown, which is now the great capital of Canada, was but a village. As history and time went on Calabogie was left behind, because when the timber resources were depleted there was nothing else there. For many years the people of Calabogie, which is fondly known as Calabogie with the blue skies above, where I come from-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
That is quite right; for many years there was nothing below. Then about ten or 12 years ago new hope came to that area-new hope of employment and new hope for a better today and an even brighter tomorrow. Iron was discovered in the area, and it was discovered to a very large extent through the study of surveys, geological and otherwise, which had been made by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys from the beginning of the century. Iron in great quantities was discovered and it appeared as though new industry and employment would come to these people.
As soon as the development of this iron reached the proportion that it was clearly commercial and profitable, in came the commercial giants, and it was not too long before the great Algoma company, under its subsidiary Algoma Ore Properties which does the developing for that corporate mining giant, had tied up all these properties which, taken together, could make a thriving commercial enterprise and give employment to the people. This was some ten or 12 years ago.
You may say, Mr. Chairman, that this is a private matter and that neither the minister nor this committee can do anything about it even after ten or 12 years. But
4838	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys I say that is not so. This corporate giant has other iron resources elsewhere which it can mine more cheaply and thus more profitably, so if anyone else wishes to develop the iron resources to give employment to the area they should be given the opportunity to do so.
Surely it should not be within the power of any corporation to control natural resources, which are the heritage of the people of the country, and not of any one company. They should not be allowed to remain in control for 50 or 100 years paying nothing but a menial tax annually in order to hold these resources instead of developing them in the interests of the people.
I suggest there is a precedent for this type of conduct which encourages corporations to develop their resources at a faster pace than at present. It was not too long ago that, as I understand, the petroleum controllers of the country were successfully urged to increase production at a faster pace than before. I am not quite certain how this was done, but I think it was Teddy Roosevelt who used to say, "Tread lightly but carry a big stick". Perhaps the minister with his affability and geniality can use the art of gentle persuasion. The big stick is legislation. However, I suggest it is in the best traditions of the party to which I have the honour to belong that over the years it has encouraged free enterprise or private enterprise, whichever you wish to call it. It has maintained the incentives and the virility of private enterprise while at the same time seeing to it that the fruits of production and the resources developed by private enterprise were used in large measure for the welfare of the people of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I have always said in this house and elsewhere that I am a man of brevity. Tonight I will show my laconic brevity. I will only say how happy I am to have this opportunity to congratulate the minister. He is a man I have known for many years. As the hon. member who has just spoken has said, he is a man of affability, a man whose attitude in this house has always won for him a high regard and warm affection. I wish him well in his portfolio. I will not say how long I hope he will be

there flourishing, but I do wish him well. He has always been a friend of mine and a sincere parliamentarian.
I am not an expert on mines. I am looking forward to hearing on this subject from my hon. friend from Bow River who knows the mining field as well as he knows the legal field. I want to commend one thing to the minister. In the province of Prince Edward Island where we derive our riches and greatness from our sterling people and wonderful soil, and where we have very little by way of minerals-we do not have many oil wells, or Kitimats, or Ungavas-we have developed a young industry to which I should like the minister to give his special attention and that is the peat moss industry in the constituency of the Solicitor General. I have recently become impressed by the potential of this new industry. I thought, at one time, it would come within the responsibility of the Department of Agriculture. At another time I thought it would come under the department of northern affairs. But I have now been truly informed that it is a responsibility of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. I ask him to lend the good offices of his department to this industry, which could mean so much for my province where we have very little at our disposal with respect to more mundane mineral wealth. I look forward to the co-operation of the department, by way of research assistance and more tangible assistance, in developments which will mean much in the economic life of Prince Edward Island.
That is all I have to say, except that I am happy to raise such an important subject in such a hopeful and optimistic field of endeavour with a minister of whom I am more hopeful and optimistic than of some of his colleagues.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I hope I shall be even more brief than the speaker who preceded me, if only to show him there are people who can be more brief than he. Besides, there is not too much to be said in connection with this particular department.
However, I should like to answer some remarks made by the hon. member for Renfrew South in connection with the attitude-he was almost ready to term it a dog-in-the-manger attitude-taken by people who were holding resources and not using them. There are two things he should know. In British Columbia they have legislation in operation which prevents this sort of thing happening. The other thing we should bear in mind in considering this question is the possibility of markets. There must be markets for any commodities we intend to produce; otherwise, what is the point of producing them?

There are great volumes of minerals present in the province of British Columbia. There certainly is no market at this time for the great volume which could be produced in that province. We have a tremendous potential. British Columbia is the province of the future in this respect, although there are many good mines in production at the present time. We have scarcely scratched the surface in British Columbia as yet.
I should like to ask the minister if he could dig up some figures. First, I should like to congratulate him on his appointment to office. I have known the hon. gentleman for a good many years now. I felt that when he was the financial critic he used to dig in pretty deep and, as a miner, possibly he will get in even deeper. I should like to ask him if he can dig up some figures on power production from coal in Wabamun, Alberta. Before this plant was built there was discussion in the house as to whether it would be cheaper to run it on coal or natural gas. I understand that the plant has converted to coal, and I would be interested in any figures the minister may have in this connection.
I would also be interested if he could tell us anything about the progress of the development of equipment designed to make economic use of coal for firing locomotives, particularly on railways. I believe this was a motor of the turbine type to be used for developing power from coal burned almost as a gas. There is another question I have in mind. I hear many complaints as I travel among the farmers of western Canada, more particularly in my own area, in connection with fertilizer. Fertilizer is a by-product of the mines in many cases and I am wondering whether or not the minister can tell us if there is a monopoly in the fertilizer industry and, if so, whether anything can be done to change that position. There seems to be a general feeling among the farmers that there is a monopoly in this industry. It has been said that though at one time fertilizer was a by-product which was thrown away it has become one of the most valuable products of the mining industry.
I have nothing more to say, though I may have some questions to ask on the estimates when they come before us in detail, should I happen to be here when they are before the committee. This is not always possible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I want first of all to join with my colleague, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, in wishing the new minister well as he takes over the responsibilities of this department and particularly as he presents these estimates to the committee for the first time.

I was pleased to hear the minister acknowledge that the estimates we are now discussing are those prepared by the former administration. I think this has made it possible to shorten the discussion considerably tonight. I am also pleased to hear him say that they are being presented without any major changes. This, it seems to me, is typical of a minister with whom I have had friendly relations over the past number of years. I think it is encouraging to those who are interested in the activities of the department to know that the work so well begun is going forward under his direction. I should also like to say that I think the minister is wise in taking this stand. There are other departments of government which have endeavoured to blaze new trails since the change of administration last April, with the result that in many instances there has had to be some retracing of steps. The policies and programs that were vigorously promoted by the government of the present Leader of the Opposition have turned out, upon closer analysis and study, to have been in the best interests of the Canadian economy.
As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has indicated, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys plays a very important part in the over-all programs of development and research in this country. Indeed, there can be no satisfactory development unless there is adequate research. Reference has already been made to the quality of the officials who serve in this important department. This is the first opportunity we have had to discuss the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys since the highly respected former deputy minister, Dr. Marc Boyer, passed away, and I should like to pay my tribute to the leadership he gave the department over a number of years. My direct association with Dr. Boyer was of rather short duration because back in 1960 I had the responsibility for this department for a short period of only two months.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: As acting minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Yes. I was not only impressed by the quality of Dr. Boyer but of all those who were associated with him. This is to be expected, I suppose, from a department whose personnel are made up largely of scientists. This is one of the unique government departments in this respect where the officials are pure scientists, not political scientists, not political artists but pure scientists who are dedicated to the pursuit of fundamental and basic research. I shall always remember carrying the responsibility for presenting the estimates of the department during that period and depending almost entirely upon those dedicated and well qualified men.

COMMONS	.
There is only one point I wish to make as I take part in this brief discussion. I wish to emphasize the importance of co-ordination and co-operation in connection with the activities of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. In his speech a few moments ago the hon. member for Renfrew South skirted around this point when he was making an appeal for some activity with regard to Calabogie. The only way that the federal Department of Mines and Technical Surveys can have any influence in regard to a problem of that kind is by ensuring that there is the closest possible co-operation with the provincial government. As we know, resources, except in the area north of 60, are the responsibility of the provincial governments. If we are going to ensure a rationalized program of national development in the resource area, it can only be achieved as the federal government and the provincial governments are willing to work together.
This afternoon I listened to a statement of the hon. member for Renfrew South with respect to another matter, and at that time he rather downgraded the importance of the new concept of co-operative federalism that was promoted with enthusiasm by the former administration. I should like to point out to the hon. member that if he wishes to have an intelligent and comprehensive resource program it can only be achieved to the extent that Ottawa is willing to work with the provinces. The machinery has already been established through the resource ministers council, and I would imagine that this new agency, which is carrying forward with such enthusiasm the new concept of co-operative federalism, would be glad to take under consideration the particular problem outlined by the hon. member for Renfrew South.
As the former minister of northern affairs and national resources I should also like to express appreciation for the close qo-operation that department has enjoyed with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. Indeed, the program of northern development could not go forward otherwise. It could not have made the tremendous and impresive advances that have been made in recent years were it not for the increased tempo of geophysical, geographical, geological and oceanographic research that has been undertaken by this important department.
The thought has been expressed from time to time that Canadians today have less pioneering spirit and are not willing to undergo the hardships involved in mastering the great land mass that we have inherited. This certainly does not apply to the officials of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys who have gone into the north, the high Arctic and the archipelago. They have

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
been carrying out research there under difficult and in some instances adverse weather conditions. I think the progress that has been made in the obtaining of information through research has been worthy of the pioneering that was done by such intrepid early northern explorers as the well known Stefansson, for example. In many instances these men have been young men.
The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has been working together with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys in other respects as well. The department of northern affairs realizing that the economy of the north depends upon the discovery, exploitation and development of mineral resources, is establishing at the present time a research co-ordination centre at Inuvik on the Arctic shore, and I am sure this will provide excellent facilities for the research programs now being carried on by the department under discussion at the present time. The department of northern affairs also encourages prospecting for minerals by prospectors' assistance programs as well as by improving the regulations.
But the one important point I should like to make is to encourage the minister. He indicated in his opening remarks that he intends to carry on in all respects the important research projects that are already under way. If I may, I should like to point to one of these as perhaps being most significant. I would draw his attention to the aerial magnetometer survey that is under way now in the northern part of the province as well as in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory. It is a ten-year program which will cost something like $18 million. I spoke in these terms last week when we had the estimates of the department of northern affairs before us. From time to time, we have heard rumblings from the government benches that there is a desire to withdraw from these joint programs. This viewpoint has been expressed in particular by the President of the Privy Council.
I would certainly hope, Mr. Chairman, that this joint program of magnetometer research that is being carried on in all of the provinces having northern regions is not one of those programs from which it is intended to withdraw. As I have pointed out, we can only proceed to develop and expand our geography as we are willing to work in the closest possible co-operation with the provinces. I hope the machinery that is already set up under the program of co-operative federalism will continue in this, as well as other areas,
and that the government, having the responsibility for administration, is willing to continue the program that has been so well begun.
These are the few remarks I should like to make at this time, Mr. Chairman. I close by once again expressing appreciation for the conciliatory and co-operative note that has been established in the discussions by the new minister. I am sure that if he will adopt that same attitude within the privy council we need have no uncertainty concerning the continuing progress of the work of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
