Now, I should like to continue in a serious vein. I am rising to speak briefly and when I say briefly I mean briefly. I have listened with interest to a number of speeches that have been made this evening. The minister, after very excellent service to the country in time of war, arrived in this house in 1945. I think we arrived here as a result of the same election. I have known him ever since he has become a member of the parliament of Canada, and to become a member of the cabinet is no mean honour. I wish him every success in all that he undertakes in fulfilling his duties as minister in charge of this department.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these estimates are not as glamorous as some with which we deal because this department is largely concerned with scientific and technical affairs. This does not mean it is not a very important department. I would be inclined to say that of all the departments this is the silent service. It renders a great service to this country, and we hear very little about it. I would criticize them to some extent in this respect because they are not as keen on using the press to advertise their own wares as some other departments are.
I rise to ask the minister a question or two and deal with a matter I have mentioned on a number of occasions through the years on these estimates. First, when the minister replies to the remarks which are made on this item, I should like him to inform the house how the programs that are undertaken by the various branches of this department are decided upon. This has always interested
4842	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys me and I have been asked to make this inquiry as the result of interest on the part of others. Second, I wish him to inform the house of the developments in connection with the studies in the Arctic. Some years ago there was a proposal made in a conference in Montreal, in 1961 I think, that there might be mutual studies made in the Arctic with scientists from the U.S.S.R. I wonder if there has been any development in that respect.
I should like now to raise the question that I particularly wanted to mention, that is the provision for the Canadian people of national daylight saving time as the result of federal-provincial co-operative agreement. In wartime, of course, the federal government had complete jurisdiction in this respect as a result of emergency circumstances. However, it seems a completely foolish thing, in my opinion and in the opinion of a good number of persons with whom I have discussed this matter, for us to have daylight saving at various times in various provinces throughout Canada. I think it would be to the great advantage of Canadians generally and to the travelling public if this matter could be brought up by the minister at a dominion-provincial conference. This matter is related to the dominion observatory item which comes under the jurisdiction of the minister. There could be an agreement between the federal government and the provinces so that we would have daylight saving established in Canada on the same day right throughout the country. I do suggest to the minister that serious consideration should be given to this technical matter. We have continued this policy of one province declaring daylight saving time on one date and another one on another date, to the inconvenience of the travelling public. I suggest that this is something upon which agreement should be easily reached.
The other matter I wanted to mention was that this department's public relations are not as good as they should be. I am not blaming the officials in the department, or the minister. A large number of Canadians are not aware of the work that is being done by this department, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I endorse what he said about the work of this department. It is surprising how few people outside of those interested in mining and certain scientific studies, know about the work of this department. I suggest there could be some consideration given to informing the Canadian people generally about the work done by this department. There are a lot of people who do not realize the services that can be provided by this department, and I


am thinking particularly with regard to the purchase of maps and reports on particular subjects.
I think some consideration should be given either to the use of press releases or the use of officials addressing local organizations, particularly those officials concerned with surveys in certain areas. This would be an excellent recess hobby for the parliamentary assistant. He could go around to the various organizations and speak about the work of this department. I think more should be done in that respect because we really could not carry on our plans for the future development of this country, for its settlement and things of that sort, without the basic studies made by various branches of this department. I just make those two or three suggestions and urge the minister to give them some consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am happy to say a few words in reference to the estimates before the committee, particularly in view of the fact that we in Alberta feel we have about one eighth of the coal supply of the whole world, and have other resources that could be mined.
Like other speakers I would like to say something in reference to the minister himself. Some of my friends urge me to be brief, and I will be brief. In fact I think I should be brief, because when I look around this chamber, particularly on the opposite side and also over on this side, it seems to me this is the way to get estimates through, in view of the number of empty seats. They speak for themselves.
The minister was one of the first members of parliament I met when I was first elected. In a kindly manner he showed me how to get to my office, what to do, and a few other things. It is that little touch of humanity that endears him not only to his own party but to the whole house. I have always been most happy that I have not been a Conservative, or a member of any other party, running in his constituency against him, because I know how difficult it must be to get elected in a contest with a man so kindly as he.
Now, I shall deal with the estimates and I have some recommendations to make. I have spoken about the coal mining industry on several occasions. There are three particular types of coal, three particular coal mining areas in the Bow River constituency. In the mountains there is found the anthracite coal which is marketed, shipped and exported to Japan. We have the bituminous coal in the foothills and the subbituminous, or soft domestic coal at Drumheller.
One of the things that has helped the coal industry was the setting up in years gone by

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
of the coal board. The industry works in conjunction with that board and I have one recommendation to make in connection with it. It has been made to other ministers, and even to our minister at the time when this party formed the government, and it is that one of the members of the united mine workers of America from western Canada should be appointed to sit on the coal board with its present members.
I believe at one time there were negotiations in the department in this regard. After all, in a day when we have such relations between management and labour, when they must work harmoniously together to be successful, this would be one way to make this industry a success, and I strongly recommend the appointment of one member from the united mine workers of America from western Canada to the coal board.
I would like to mention some of the difficulties affecting the coal industry of western Canada, and in particular the industry in Bow River. As the minister is well aware, and he has been in this house longer than I, the coal industry has run into serious competition with the petroleum industry in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. At one time large quantities of coal were used by the railroads, and as domestic fuel on the farms and in the urban centres. Today it has been supplanted by natural gas, petroleum or other by-products and as a result the industry has been, to put it midly, dislocated and disturbed.
Alberta boasts of being one of the richest provinces in Canada, but there are areas in that province in which the most dire poverty exists. I have said this before and I want to emphasize it again. These miners were just as great pioneers as the farmers and other people who came to western Canada. They went great distances underground, at the risk of their lives, to mine coal so that the other pioneers as they developed western Canada had the use of that resource, particularly during the long winters, in their development work.
I have said to the Minister of Justice, to the minister of northern affairs and to other ministers, that in this welfare state, about which sometimes I have a lot to say, many basic welfare programs do not apply to the miner who has been unemployed for a long time. He is usually a man aged about 45, 50 or 55 years and he becomes unemployed long before he qualifies for old age security. He has no chance to get other kinds of employment. As a result of his long employment he cannot get unemployment insurance, and social welfare is not sufficient to maintain his family in dignity.
28902-5-309
With a great sense of hospitality I invite the minister-and I trust it will be soon-to visit that area of the Drumheller valley which is rich in farmland, but very poor so far as mining is concerned. I invite him to visit such towns as Wayne, Rosedale, Macmine and Newcastle, which I might describe as lit up cemeteries. There are people living there in what might be called hovels, with no basis of income whatsoever because, as I have said and I am going to repeat, they have no unemployment insurance and have very little social welfare.
One might ask, why do they not leave these areas? Well, if they leave, they leave what little capital they have created, their homes and other buildings, and they are only fitted and trained for one particular vocation, and that is mining.
I have not the figures before me, but I have quoted them often enough and I am sure I will give them correctly. Some time just after the last war there were 26 mines open in that area, employing more than 2,000 men. Today I believe there are three mines left in that area and I am given to understand-and this is no criticism of the Liberal government because I am certain it would have happened even if the Conservatives had been in power-another mine is about to close. This is part of the evolution and development of other energy sources, but as a result the mines now employ only about 180 men, and when this mine closes there will be only 100 employed.
I do not know how many of the 2,000 original miners are still in that area, but as I say, as one drives through these places they are like lit up cemeteries. After leaving that mining area one can then drive into the farm region of Bow River and Acadia, which is represented by my hon. friend behind me, and these have some of the richest agricultural land anywhere in western Canada.
Yet there is this small area crowded with people living in poverty. One can look at all that is being done for the agricultural industry. Every one of us has supported the steps taken to help it, but now the time has come to do something to help these people. Nothing has been done for them provincially. I am not criticizing the provincial government in that regard, and decidedly nothing definite has been done federally to assist them.
A lot of these people came to that area during the last world war. There was a demand for the type of fuel produced in it, and it was needed for the war effort. Men were brought from Nova Scotia and other coal mining areas to Drumheller and dumped there, but when the mines folded the men
4844	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys were left unemployed. They need some definite plan of assistance to help them in reference to the plight in which they now find themselves.
Of course during the last few years we have found a new market for anthracite coal. The subvention on anthracite was increased to $4.50 a ton, and as a result in one year we were able to export 700,000 tons to Japan. I believe that figure was duplicated in another year, and the export of it is still continuing. There is no doubt that many of those miners, situated in what we call the Drumheller area, moved to Can-more, Alberta, but as I pointed out there is a saturation point, and there are only so many of those people who can be moved and can be employed by coal operators in the Canmore area. We have a new minister of this department and I ask him as earnestly as I can to find some plan to help these people. I have said once before in this house that if I never did anything as a member of parliament, if I never made any contribution at all to my country, and I could make one contribution in being partly responsible for these people receiving help from any Canadian government, I would feel I had made a real contribution as a member of this house.
While I am dealing with the competition that exists in petroleum and natural gas, I would point out that there is this type of thing to consider. At one time many of the natural gas wells-and I see the hon. member for Coast-Capilano on the other side of the chamber, who is well aware of this subject and appreciates what I am saying-were found when they were drilling for oil, and the wells were capped. We had the Borden report. We found that in the province of Alberta alone we had proven reserves of 23.7 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. This was not estimated; it was proven. We needed for Canada's needs in the foreseeable future, not only for domestic needs, projecting it over 30 years, an average of 12 billion cubic feet per year. After the report and after the energy board was set up, for the first time in Canada we started to export natural gas.
Practically every urban centre in Alberta, and even many farms in that province, is today heated by natural gas. These farms used to use domestic coal. Those that are not near a gas pipe line are today using other by-products of the petroleum industry. Therefore the market for soft fuels throughout western Canada has gone. They are in competition with natural gas and petroleum. That competition is so great that it has put operators out of business; and when business goes, there are no jobs. I have spoken to these people many times. They belong to a union, and they sometimes had very radical ideas.


I have pointed out to them-and I am sure hon. members of all parties will agree with me on this-that unless the operators themselves are able to show a profit, there cannot be jobs for them. They now appreciate the fact that as the operation disappears, so employment disappears. I do not want to emphasize this, but once again I would ask the minister to do something to help these people. I saw him making a note in his usual kindly manner and know he will give consideration to my request. I sincerely hope that a member of the united mine workers of America from western Canada will, for the first time in Canada, be appointed to the coal board so these people can express their ideas about the industry and their ideas as far as their relationships with management are concerned.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to turn to one other aspect of this question for a few moments. I have only two points to discuss tonight. I shall now deal with the question of the north. I say this again in a kindly way: There are some people in the house who used to scoff at the previous government when we talked about the vision of the north. I am not one of those who believe that the first government to ever get people to go to the north or industry to become interested in the north was a Conservative government, but I think even the present Liberals will accept-they may accept it because it would have happened anyway

that there has certainly been great development in the north. Whatever way you look at it, that is the fact.
I have here a map of Canada, and particularly a map of our northern area. I want to ask one serious question. I think the minister or the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources should take a serious look at this question. I was a member of the mines committee in 1958-59 when that committee considered this very subject. I recall asking one question in that committee, "Where is the border of northern Canada?" I am sure that there is not an oceanographer or any other kind of scientist up there who can say we could draw a line tonight between what might belong to a foreign state and what might belong to Canada in that area. This is an important matter. When the oceanographers and hydrographers came before the committee and were asked certain questions in reference to their work, we found out-perhaps there has been an improvement in this situation-that at that time their salary was less than that of a topnotch stenographer in a good oil company in the city of Calgary. How can we expect to attract people to the civil service to undertake these important scientific jobs if we do not pay the salary they are worth? Some of them were

at university for as long as 10 or 12 years and then had practical experience of three or four years. At that time I think we had two oceanographers working in the department. Consider this in relation to the size of northern Canada. I think we had two other scientists working in reference to the boundaries. The committee will appreciate how inadequate this is compared to the size of northern Canada.
My second suggestion is this. If we have not the financial resources to complete the vision that we have, whoever created it, for the development of the north-and I think we made a great contribution in that regard: perhaps I am prejudiced, but I think we did -we should make some kind of deal with our friends outside the iron curtain, to make certain that we develop the north to such an extent that we push back those boundaries in order that we on this side of the iron curtain control the majority of the northern hemisphere.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
We have done quite well, when you think of it. When you look at the map, you find we have now started to drill wells as far north as Banks island and Bathurst island, and there is some development going on in Ellesmere island. We know there is some development going on by the Americans under that part which is called the ice shield; they are going under this area in submarines. But we should work in conjunction with these people, because this is really the northern boundary as far as Canada is concerned. The more we develop it, the further north we push industry, the further our borders will extend to the north.
Most of us believe that we own all the north, but those foreign countries which have started development on the islands in this northern area will not be pushed out in the near future because we get into the niceties of an argument or set up an international commission that says, "This is Canada's land; you should not have drilled these wells". I believe-and I have the figures here-that the total potential world development at the present time, of known crude petroleum, is 273 billion barrels. Of these 273 billion barrels of known crude petroleum, we in Alberta have projected reserves of 5 billion barrels. It is believed that there are probably 100 billion barrels of crude petroleum which could be developed in the far north. I say that, now we have started this development in the north, let us not allow it to lag. I recall that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, the former minister of northern affairs and national resources, endeavoured to sell their cabinet on the development of the north 28902-5-309i
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys and did a good job in the vision of developing that part of our country. Let us keep that development going, because this does not only mean development in the northern part of Canada; it means a great deal to the whole of Canada. When these industries are developed it will mean what eastern industrial centres mean to western Canada in relation to their industrial products; because they are the manufacturers, they are the ones who sell the commodities being developed from these resources. I say, Mr. Chairman, that this vision should be carried on, that this development should be carried on and encouraged.
I was rather amused to hear my hon. friend talk about their sharing the riches. In that connection I just wish to point this out. Many of us have always accepted the idea, except a few who seem to be diminishing in number day by day-the intellectual type of socialism does not seem to be around anymore, or the ones who seem to think they are real socialists do not seem to be around anymore-that things can be done better under free enterprise. However, you have only to look at what the Borden report says-although I will not name the trans-Canada pipe line-about sharing the riches. I think free enterprise is everyone having the same opportunity to compete. I recall particularly in one place the Borden report stated that one man made a capital gain out of receiving shares-he was an executive of a crown company at that time-worth $1,400,000, and still got 10,000 shares in another comDany at $8, which at the time he took the certificates were worth about $34.50. If that is the kind of free enterprise we are talking about, I am sure it is not the kind the hon. member for Renfrew South was talking about. Free enterprise means that all people have the opportunity to go in and develop.
I raised this question on the budget debate when special tax rights were given to certain pipe line companies. I said that if special privileges and taxes were given to pipe line companies to drill a hole for petroleum in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba or in the north, why could they not be given to any company or any syndicate that wished to pour money into it and explore for petroleum in the north or on the prairies? I was told that this would be soliciting business for people who wanted to get rich and live in suburban areas. Surely, if it is fair for the pipe line companies to have that kind of tax exemption, it would be fair for members sitting across from me now, who are smiling, to form a syndicate and put our money in. And if it was a dry hole, why should we not get exemption on our tax forms, the same as a pipe line company? It is that kind of thing that will develop the country. But every time
4846	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys we give out special privileges we are putting hobbles on those people who would develop the country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: What about M.P.'s selling oil stocks?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I hear someone talking about M.P.'s selling oil stocks. The most refreshing thing I heard this evening was the hon. gentleman talking about free enterprise in such glowing terms that I knew we had won him over after all. He used to speak only in socialistic terms when I first came here. He was one of the intellectual, honest socialists. Either his philosophy has faded or he finds it more popular to follow along with free enterprise. I think that is the best answer I can give to that interruption.
The best comparison is this, that you only have to compare the economy of the province of Alberta with that of Saskatchewan to have the answer. There is one thing which I will say about this government. They say more oil; but I was glad to have the question put to me. What happened to the oil rigs in 1944 when the socialists took over? They left Saskatchewan and went to an economic climate where they could do business. When they found oil they at least knew they could share it and the royalties with the government. Saskatchewan had a good plan, one of the finest in the world. They were told to risk their capital and to do the research with their seismographs, and all the rest of it. They were told: "You build a well and we'll own the oil". But that was not too appealing to the average Canadian and the average American, so they left for Alberta. Now my good friends, with that kind of program, say to me: "Why have you so much petroleum in the province of Alberta?" I pay that government the greatest compliment I can pay them. During the years they were in office they created the proper economic climate for the development of the province, which I think accounts for the reason they are rich today, whereas in mines and resources Saskatchewan is still struggling.
I recall reading in Maclean's magazine some years ago about the "hottest square mile in the world". I did not know what they were talking about, but they were talking about uranium. That uranium was mined by a crown corporation. The hottest square mile in the world in 1947 was the square mile that brought in Leduc No. 1 which developed the petroleum which made the province of Alberta rich. The proper economic climate was there. Some people tell me that the backbenchers of the Liberal party today are all left-wingers. Then someone else whispers that they are all right-wingers. But whichever it is, I hope they influence their government to


stay on the trail of free enterprise, because without it another group of people will take over control. What happened in Saskatchewan could happen throughout Canada, and I hope that will not be the plaque left with the Liberals of today. I trust that there are enough free enterprisers left over on that side to make certain that their left-wingers do not get control.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I should like to add a few
words to the discussion, but I shall be very brief. First of all I want to add a word to those of others concerning the new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. I have known him ever since I became a member of the house and I have the greatest personal admiration for him. I wish him every success as minister during the length of time he holds that office. I also wish to pay another compliment to him. It was my good fortune to recommend to the former government that we start subventions on coal shipments to Japan. That program has worked out very successfully, and over the past five years of operation has gradually grown. The operators have been feeling their way. Tests have been made as to the value of coal for metallurgical purposes, and apparently it is excellent when mixed with Japanese coal. Therefore Japanese processors have come back year after year with new contracts for our coal.
In order that our mine operators could operate efficiently it became evident that we should give them a longer period in which to adjust their contracts and also solicit new business. We had meeting after meeting among the operators on that very point, as well as among the miners. I suggested that the subsidy on coal to Japan should be extended by at least five years so that these operators would be able to do an efficient job of planning. I am pleased to see that the present minister has extended that subvention for a five-year term. It is a very good move.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: We intend to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I understood it had been.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: No, it is promised. We need legislation to do it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I see. Your intention is to do so. Thank you. I hope it will be extended, because these people need that additional time in order to make their plans for the future. The Crowsnest pass area has recently been designated as a slow growth area. It is the only area in Alberta which has been so designated and any help which the minister can give to assist it by way of new industries or coal subventions or the development of projects which would utilize coal, natural gas, iron ore, or forest products

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
which are so abundant in this area would go a long way toward providing jobs for the people there. Such assistance is needed in the development of that district.
I should like to say to the minister in closing that we would like him to come out and visit us. I can say personally I would be glad to take him in my car down to the Crowsnest area and if it happens to be the shooting season, I can guarantee him some good shooting down on my place.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: You would be a good companion.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Who is going to shoot whom?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: I do appreciate the minister's efforts in extending this subvention on coal and I will certainly support the measure when he brings it to the floor of the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
I wonder if the committee would bear with me for a few moments. I am one of those members who have been associated with the present minister since 1949- that is, with some breaks, although I have kept in touch with him throughout all those years. I want to add my congratulations on his appointment. I am not going to suppose he will do a good job. I know he is doing a good job, judging by actions he has already taken.
I think, also, that in view of the fact that I am perhaps the only member registered as a miner in the Parliamentary Guide, it would be appropriate for me to say just a few words. The hon. member for Macleod mentioned the subsidy on coal shipments to Japan. I wish to say this has been a very successful operation. On June 26 the minister did announce that the coal subvention policy would be continued for five years. On that understanding the coal operators in the pass area have already signed a three-year agreement. Previously the agreement had been on a one-year basis. The operators have now signed a three year agreement for 600,000 tons, in this particular area alone. The contract provides, also, that they may increase this amount by 100,000 tons a year, which would make it 800,000 tons from the Crowsnest pass area. I would hope to have the support of members of this committee in urging upon the government the desirability of raising the ceiling upon which they are prepared to pay this subsidy. These shipments are having an admirable effect on the economy of British Columbia generally, because of the number of jobs they generate in addition to the employment in the mines themselves. So I hope a policy of increasing the ceiling on the amount of coal which may be shipped under the terms of the subvention will be adopted.
The hon. member for Macleod has said the Crowsnest pass area is the only area in Alberta which has been designated as a slow growth area. I want to remind the committee that it includes a portion of British Columbia which is being served by the Blairmore unemployment insurance office, so Fernie, Natal and Michel are towns which are receiving assistance because of this subvention.
That is all I want to say on that subject. As a miner, I am also connected with a company which produces fertilizer and I wish to assure the hon. member for Cariboo that the fertilizer industry is not a monopoly. It is one of the most highly competitive industries that exists today. There is some connection between the fertilizer industry and the mining industry, but not in every respect. A great deal of fertilizer is produced on the prairies through using natural gas. The industry is by far and away the least monopolistic in Canada today. I feel the department itself is doing an excellent job. There is one industry in my riding to which it has directed a great deal of attention. We have hundreds of millions of tons of iron which has already been mined, and which is now stockpiled in the form of concentrates ready to be made into steel. It was with the assistance of the department, after it had conducted a number of tests and experiments, that we finally developed a steel which could be produced from this ore. It is the beginning of a great steel industry in this area. It might well become the the Pittsburgh of Canada. I wish to thank the department for its assistance. I just thought that because I am a miner I should say a few words on these estimates.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
The great district of Athabasca is one of the neglected areas of Canada and it is hard for me to understand why. We are worried today about the balance of international payments. I sincerely believe that if one resource in the Athabasca district alone were to be developed, its crude oil, we could largely take care of that whole problem.
The question of pipe lines causes many eyebrows to be raised. I do not intend to add my voice by raising any recriminations about pipe lines which have been built. I will only say it is high time we built a pipe line from Alberta to Montreal to carry crude oil. If that were done, and if we had protection for the market in Montreal, we could go into full time production of crude oil from the Athabasca tar sands. I can say that the known reserves in the tar sands in that area alone amount to more than 300 billion barrels of oil. So far they are completely untapped. If they were tapped we could supply the whole of the heavy industrial fuel oil market of eastern Canada. In order for this to be done it would not be enough to build a pipe line.
4848	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys We must protect the market. This would mean placing restrictions on the importation of Venezuela crude.
There are not too many people today who are brave enough to face the oil combines of the world. Perhaps we can; I do not know. I would like to try. I see no reason at all why we cannot protect our markets in Canada, as well as other countries can protect theirs. It has been the policy not only of Conservative but of Liberal governments in Canada as well to protect our own local markets, and here we have a market for industrial fuel oil alone which would bring in several hundred million dollars to the exchequer of Canada, and the payrolls of our people.
The time is long overdue for the building of a crude oil pipe line from Alberta. If it cannot be built with private funds then it should be built with government funds because in this way we would be developing our own country. There is a great deal of talk about Canadianism, biculturalism and a square deal all round. If we got down to brass tacks and developed our country in the way it should be developed we would not have to worry about a square deal all round. We would have to bring in workers from all over the world to take up the slack. There would be no unemployment if we would only get down to developing our own resources and looking after our own markets.
I should like to close with a compliment to the department for their wonderful work in technical surveys. There are new developments in air surveys and I think that in the near future we will have a much clearer picture of what our resources in the north are. I think that parliament should vote almost a blank cheque to technical surveys so that they may show us what we have in our own country. When we know what we have we can take the logical steps for development.
I also want to pay my personal respects to the new minister. Although he is a senior member of the house he has always looked upon backbenchers like myself almost in a fatherly way, and we appreciate this. It is an example of the kind of comradeship we need throughout the house if we are going to develop our country in an efficient manner.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are quite a number of items in connection with this department about which I wish to speak and some questions I wish to put to the minister. In northwestern Ontario at the present time, where mining is part of the basic economic structure, there is a certain amount of optimism due to the fact that the minister of mines of Ontario represents Port Arthur and right next door we have the federal Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys representing Kenora-Rainy River. If that were not


enough, next door in Fort William we have the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works. So there is considerable optimism that with all this power, we will have some attention paid to our interests, particularly in the mining field.
The reason for this hopefulness, of course, stems from the fact that most of the people in our region in looking forward to the future have to recognize that the opportunities of expanding at all in the direction of value of product or in range or variety of product in the forest industries are quite limited, whereas the prospects in the mineral industries are much more open, not only on the basis of future discovery but also on the basis of what has been blocked out already. It is for that reason I want to bring to the attention of the minister publicly, not in a niggling or needling sense and not really to tell him something he does not know, some of the matters that are of interest in our area.
The first one is somewhat esoteric, and I put it forward to begin with since it does not involve a great deal of detail and really is a matter of optimism, I suppose, or idealism in connection with the mining industry. I should like to make an appeal to the minister to do something substantial for the prospectors in this country. I make the point to the minister that this particular department has been expanding its facilities and the kind of contribution it makes to delineating our mineral resources and mapping and surveying. Traditionally in their printed form the department's publications and contributions have been most useful. I know I once looked after a library in Port Arthur that had a set of the geological surveys from 1842 up to 1930 and it always amazed me. You never knew what time of the day or evening you would get a telephone call from a prospector wanting to look at these reports. As a matter of fact, it was the use of one report in connection with Manitouwadge that led to the interest, follow-up and discovery of Geco and the very large property there.
I get complaints repeatedly, particularly from the prospectors association in Port Arthur and Fort William, about the fact that there is really no provision at all for support by the federal government in this field. Yet more and more the kinds of publication and surveys that the department is turning out are getting to be beyond usefulness so far as many of the prospectors are concerned who are not supported by the big syndicates. It is quite apparent that the whole trend in this field is toward scientific elaboration. You have these very large corporations which, partly because of the tax incentives involved, spend a great deal of money exploring and

following up all the leads that are opened up both by the federal mining service and the provincial mining service.
I am not quarrelling with this. Some of the results have been very good. But the opportunities for the ordinary person who is interested in mining, the kind of people who go to the provincial prospectors' schools, the kind of people who will go out after the big companies have been through an area with their magnetometer surveys and have made the other kinds of readings that are made from an aircraft, the kind of people who cover the area on the ground, are becoming more limited. In my view this is still a very important part of prospecting in this country. At the present time these people have no incentive at all. They have no subsidies of any kind. I believe the province of Saskatchewan has some kind of arrangement which I understand has been successful. I think there is some semi-arrangement in British Columbia and I believe there is one in prospect in Manitoba.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext: Northern affairs too.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Northern affairs, yes, but that is not in the provinces and it does not affect the part of the country in which I am interested. I think the most exciting thing the minister could do, and one which would make the memory of his period in this portfolio a happy one which would last for a long time, would be to introduce some kind of program-I am not talking about anything huge or extravagant-under which the federal government would contribute in association with the provincial government to the support of prospectors.
What is a prospector? It seems to me he is a man who will go out and search, search and search, always looking for the dream. I have a prospector friend who is 73. He lives alone. I would say that for nine months of the year, provided the weather permits, he is out prospecting. He is always looking for the mother lode, the big strike. A couple of times he thought he had it. A few years ago he thought he had something north of Armstrong that was going to be another Sudbury, but unfortunately it turned out to be just a single plug that came up.
But it is that kind of person we need. We have a great many prospectors in our part of the country who are in their 60's and 70's and who are beginning to fall away and we have not got young people in the 30's and 40's with the same incentive. I suggest there is a real field here for a certain kind of person that we produce in our bush country, people who do not have to have a great deal of technical education but who have the
Business of the House
know-how, a sense of the bush and the lakes, a practical man's knowledge of rocks, and who can cover the countryside with an intensity that even the great big surveys cannot match. Before I call it 10.30 I should like to add that the minister could really make a contribution if he would get some kind of program under way in this field.

On Monday we will consider the second reading stage of the act to amend the Technical and Vocational Training Act; then, we will consider the resolution preceding the amendments to the National Centennial Act. When that is disposed of, we will consider the resolution preceding the amendments to the Admiralty Act; then, the resolution preceding the Canadian National Railways Financing Act. If there is any time left, we will take the second reading stage of the act to amend the Bankruptcy Act and the second reading stage of the act to repeal the Newfoundland Savings Bank Act, 1939.
On Tuesday, we will consider the first three items I mentioned which have not been concluded and then, the three resolutions in the name of the Minister of Transport, namely item No. 16 on today's order paper, the railway grade crossing fund; item No. 17, the St. Lawrence Seaway Act and item No. 20, the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation Act.
